Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] High-rate Matrix room/member enumeration against tchap.gouv.fr from single client
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] PowerShell scripts embedding hardcoded LDAP credentials (Tchap-style leak)
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] First-time endpoint connection to Tchap homeserver (tchap.gouv.fr) for a user
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Bulk download from Tchap homeserver to single endpoint (media/attachment exfil)
First-time endpoint connection to Tchap homeserver (tchap.gouv.fr) for a user AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for the first observation of a given user/device pair establishing connectivity to the Tchap Matrix homeserver after a 30-day baseline. Useful as a low-noise pivot for SOCs whose users normally do NOT touch Tchap, and as a 'new device for compromised account' signal where they do. Rationale: Article names tchap.gouv.fr and matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr as the only platform endpoints. A baseline anti-join keeps noise low even in heavy-Tchap-use orgs by surfacing new (user, device) pairs that just started touching the homeserver. Cross-checked attribution against BleepingComputer's writeup and DINUM's incident notice referenced in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/french-govt-says-tchap-breach-affected-over-73-000-accounts/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/
ATT&CKT1078 T1566
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Newly onboarded French civil servant logging into Tchap from a freshly imaged laptop
  • Existing user installing Tchap on a second device (phone-to-laptop migration)
  • VPN/proxy exit-node change causing the first observation through a new corporate egress
  • Penetration testers or threat-hunters validating Tchap reachability
  • Browser pre-fetch / link-preview engines resolving tchap.gouv.fr from email-scanning gateways
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msedge.exe", "chrome.exe") or ConnectionCount > 5
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the user is a legitimate Tchap user (French public-sector role); check identity provider for recent password reset, MFA changes, or anomalous SignInLogs entries; pull EmailEvents for the same UPN over the past 7 days looking for Tchap-themed lures from external senders. 2) Contain: If user is non-Tchap or login geo/UA is anomalous, force credential reset, revoke active Tchap session via DINUM portal, isolate the device. 3) Hunt: Pivot on the same DeviceId for follow-on PowerShell with LDAP strings, bulk media downloads (/\_matrix/media/), and outbound transfers >100 MB to tchap domains in the next 24h.
let lookback = 1d;
let baseline = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(31d) .. ago(lookback))
    | where RemoteUrl has_any ("tchap.gouv.fr", "matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr")
    | summarize by DeviceId, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("tchap.gouv.fr", "matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| join kind=leftanti baseline on DeviceId, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            ConnectionCount = count(),
            Hosts = make_set(RemoteUrl, 5),
            Clients = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 5)
            by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn
| order by FirstSeen desc
let lookback = 1d;
let baseline = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(31d) .. ago(lookback))
    | where Url has_any ("tchap.gouv.fr", "matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr")
    | summarize by SrcHostname, SrcUsername;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Url has_any ("tchap.gouv.fr", "matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr")
| join kind=leftanti baseline on SrcHostname, SrcUsername
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            ConnectionCount = count(),
            Hosts = make_set(Url, 5)
            by SrcHostname, SrcUsername, SrcIpAddr
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.defender) (@EventID:3 OR @EventID:22) (@DestinationHostname:(*tchap.gouv.fr OR *TCHAP.GOUV.FR) OR @QueryName:(*tchap.gouv.fr OR *TCHAP.GOUV.FR))
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(^|\.)tchap\.gouv\.fr$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=[min(@timestamp, as=FirstSeen), count(as=Hits)])
| FirstSeen >= (now() - 86400000)
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic where Network_Traffic.dest like "%tchap.gouv.fr" earliest=-1d by Network_Traffic.src Network_Traffic.user Network_Traffic.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Network_Traffic)` | join type=left src user [| tstats summariesonly=true count as baselineHits from datamodel=Network_Traffic where Network_Traffic.dest like "%tchap.gouv.fr" earliest=-31d latest=-1d by Network_Traffic.src Network_Traffic.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Network_Traffic)`] | where isnull(baselineHits) OR baselineHits=0
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic where Network_Traffic.dest like "%tchap.gouv.fr" earliest=-1d by Network_Traffic.src Network_Traffic.user Network_Traffic.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Network_Traffic)` | join type=left src user [| tstats summariesonly=false count as baselineHits from datamodel=Network_Traffic where Network_Traffic.dest like "%tchap.gouv.fr" earliest=-31d latest=-1d by Network_Traffic.src Network_Traffic.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Network_Traffic)`] | where isnull(baselineHits) OR baselineHits=0
High-rate Matrix room/member enumeration against tchap.gouv.fr from single client AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects a single endpoint or account issuing a burst of Matrix client-server API calls (rooms, members, joined_members, sync, publicRooms) to the Tchap homeserver — the exact scraping pattern 'Misère' used to enumerate 73,467 accounts and 650,000 messages from unencrypted public rooms. Rationale: Article explicitly states the actor 'scraped nearly 650,000 messages and information from more than 73,000 accounts' from unencrypted public rooms — only Matrix client-server endpoints like /rooms, /joined_members, /members, /publicRooms, /sync can produce that. Kill-chain phase 3 (T1087/T1083) names /sync and /members as the discovery hints. Threshold 500 calls in 5 min picks up sustained scraping while staying above normal client polling. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/french-govt-says-tchap-breach-affected-over-73-000-accounts/ • https://spec.matrix.org/v1.10/client-server-api/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087/
ATT&CKT1087 T1083 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Tchap mobile/desktop client cold-starting and bulk-syncing a heavy user with hundreds of rooms
  • Federation backfill after a homeserver outage when a busy account reconnects
  • Internal automation / chatbot integration polling Tchap via API for audit
  • DINUM-run pen-test or red-team exercises against the platform
  • SOAR/SIEM integration scraping Tchap for content moderation
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("element.exe", "tchap.exe", "riot.exe") or ApiCalls > 2000
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm whether the source UPN is a known Tchap automation/bot account (chatbot, archiver); check whether the account is one DINUM has flagged or blocked; pull AADSignInEventsBeta / IdentityLogonEvents for the same UPN for unusual geo/ASN. 2) Contain: If unsanctioned, request DINUM block the account on Tchap (matching their public statement that they blocked the offending account); revoke OAuth/access tokens; quarantine the source IP at the perimeter. 3) Hunt: Search for subsequent bulk media downloads (UC4), egress to /_matrix/media/, and outbound transfers > 1 GB to Tchap domains across the same UPN/IP for the prior 30 days.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteUrl has "tchap.gouv.fr"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/_matrix/client", "/rooms", "/joined_members", "/members", "/publicRooms", "/sync")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize ApiCalls = count(),
            DistinctUrls = dcount(RemoteUrl),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            SampleUrls = make_set(RemoteUrl, 10)
            by bin(Timestamp, 5m), DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, InitiatingProcessFileName
| where ApiCalls > 500 and DistinctUrls > 50
| extend BurstSeconds = datetime_diff('second', LastSeen, FirstSeen)
| order by ApiCalls desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where Url has "tchap.gouv.fr"
| where Url has_any ("/_matrix/client", "/rooms", "/joined_members", "/members", "/publicRooms", "/sync")
| summarize ApiCalls = count(),
            DistinctUrls = dcount(Url),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            SampleUrls = make_set(Url, 10)
            by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m), SrcHostname, SrcUsername, SrcIpAddr
| where ApiCalls > 500 and DistinctUrls > 50
| order by ApiCalls desc
source:(windows.sysmon OR proxy) (@DestinationHostname:(*tchap.gouv.fr OR *TCHAP.GOUV.FR) OR @http.url:(*tchap.gouv.fr/_matrix/* OR *TCHAP.GOUV.FR/_matrix/*)) (@http.url:(*\/rooms* OR *\/joined_members* OR *\/members* OR *\/publicRooms* OR *\/sync*))
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| join({#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/tchap\.gouv\.fr$/i | groupBy([aid, FirstIP4Record], function=count())}, field=[aid, RemoteAddressIP4], include=[DomainName])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, bin(@timestamp, 5m)], function=count(as=ApiCalls))
| ApiCalls > 500
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Web where Web.url like "%tchap.gouv.fr%" AND (Web.url like "%/_matrix/client/%/rooms%" OR Web.url like "%/joined_members%" OR Web.url like "%/members%" OR Web.url like "%/publicRooms%" OR Web.url like "%/sync%") by _time span=5m Web.src Web.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where count > 500
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.url like "%tchap.gouv.fr%" AND (Web.url like "%/_matrix/client/%/rooms%" OR Web.url like "%/joined_members%" OR Web.url like "%/members%" OR Web.url like "%/publicRooms%" OR Web.url like "%/sync%") by _time span=5m Web.src Web.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where count > 500
PowerShell scripts embedding hardcoded LDAP credentials (Tchap-style leak) AIWeaponization High
Hunts for PowerShell processes whose command line or script body embeds an LDAP:// bind URI together with a password/bind credential — the same secret pattern the Tchap attacker harvested from a .ps1 file shared in a public room. Catches both pre-existing local exposure and ingested copies of the leaked script. Rationale: Article specifically calls out 'hardcoded LDAP credentials leaked via a PowerShell script' — the highest-fidelity artefact in the entire incident. Regex requires BOTH an LDAP:// URI AND a credential-shaped keyword on the same command line, which keeps FPs low; the DeviceFileEvents arm catches the leaked script being re-introduced into the environment via Tchap downloads (FileOriginUrl). Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/french-govt-says-tchap-breach-affected-over-73-000-accounts/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/001/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/iads/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate AD administration scripts (e.g. Get-ADUser bootstrap) that hardcode service-account bind credentials for scheduled tasks
  • Vendor product installers (Quest, ManageEngine) that embed test LDAP URIs in setup wizards
  • Identity-governance one-shot scripts run from a jump host with bind password in the args
  • DSC/Ansible runs that pass plaintext LDAP credentials on the command line
  • Pen-testers' Invoke-Mimikatz / PowerView showcase runs in a lab
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("vscode.exe","devenv.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("explorer.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: Capture the full ProcessCommandLine and source .ps1 file via DeviceFileEvents (SHA256, FolderPath, FileOriginUrl). Determine whether the LDAP bind DN points at a real directory and whether the password is currently valid. 2) Contain: Immediately rotate the exposed LDAP bind credential; revoke any AD service accounts referenced; if the script came from Tchap (FileOriginUrl match), assume the secret is already in the attacker's possession and treat it as compromised. 3) Hunt: Pivot on the bind DN — search SecurityEvent EventID 4624/4769 for any logons using that account in the last 30 days; check ldap.* connections from atypical hosts; review DeviceFileEvents for other copies of the same SHA256 across the fleet.
let suspectScripts = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "powershell_ise.exe") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe")
    | where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)LDAP://[^\s\"']+"
    | where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(password|pwd|bindpassword|secret|cn\s*=\s*[^,]+,\s*dc\s*=)\s*[=:]?\s*\S{4,}"
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName, AccountUpn,
              FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256;
let droppedFromTchap = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName endswith ".ps1" or FileName endswith ".psm1"
    | where FileOriginUrl has_any ("tchap.gouv.fr", "matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, FileOriginUrl,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, SHA256;
suspectScripts
| union kind=outer droppedFromTchap
| order by Timestamp desc
let suspectScripts = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell_ise.exe"
    | where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)LDAP://[^\s\"']+"
    | where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(password|pwd|bindpassword|secret|cn\s*=\s*[^,]+,\s*dc\s*=)\s*[=:]?\s*\S{4,}"
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, AccountName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName;
let droppedFromTchap = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where TargetFileName endswith ".ps1" or TargetFileName endswith ".psm1"
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("tchap.gouv.fr", "matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr")
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, FileName, FilePath, ProcessName;
suspectScripts
| union kind=outer droppedFromTchap
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: PowerShell Process Hardcoded LDAP Bind Credentials
id: 8b3f9c2e-1d4a-4f6e-9b22-7c1e54a83af1
description: Detects PowerShell process command lines that embed an LDAP:// bind URI together with a password/bind keyword and a credential-shaped token, matching the hardcoded LDAP secret pattern leaked via a PowerShell script in the June 2026 Tchap breach.
references:
    - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/french-govt-says-tchap-breach-affected-over-73-000-accounts/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/001/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/12
tags:
    - attack.credential_access
    - attack.t1552.001
    - attack.execution
    - attack.t1059.001
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\powershell_ise.exe'
    selection_ldap_uri:
        CommandLine|re: '(?i)LDAP://[^\s\"'']+'
    selection_secret:
        CommandLine|re: '(?i)(password|pwd|bindpassword|secret)\s*[=:]\s*\S{4,}'
    filter_machine:
        User|endswith: '$'
    condition: selection_image and selection_ldap_uri and selection_secret and not filter_machine
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate Active Directory administration scripts that intentionally hardcode bind credentials (a poor practice, but treat as exposure)
    - Vendor product installers that embed LDAP test strings
level: high
source:(windows.security OR windows.sysmon) (@EventID:1 OR @EventID:4688) (@Image:(*\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\PWSH.EXE) OR @NewProcessName:(*\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\pwsh.exe)) (@CommandLine:(*LDAP\:\/\/* OR *ldap\:\/\/*)) (@CommandLine:(*password* OR *Password* OR *PASSWORD* OR *pwd* OR *bindpassword* OR *BindPassword* OR *ConvertTo-SecureString*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh|powershell_ise)\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)LDAP://[^\\s\"']+", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(?i)(password|pwd|bindpassword|secret|cn\\s*=\\s*[^,]+,\\s*dc\\s*=)\\s*[=:]?\\s*\\S{4,}", field=CommandLine)
| UserName!=/\$$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=[min(@timestamp, as=FirstSeen), count(as=Hits)])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="powershell.exe" OR Processes.process_name="pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process=*LDAP://* AND (Processes.process="*password*" OR Processes.process="*pwd*" OR Processes.process="*bindpassword*" OR Processes.process="*ConvertTo-SecureString*") by Processes.user Processes.dest Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | regex process="(?i)LDAP://[^\s\"\']+" | regex process="(?i)(password|pwd|bindpassword|secret)\s*[=:]\s*\S{4,}"
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="powershell.exe" OR Processes.process_name="pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process=*LDAP://* AND (Processes.process="*password*" OR Processes.process="*pwd*" OR Processes.process="*bindpassword*" OR Processes.process="*ConvertTo-SecureString*") by Processes.user Processes.dest Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | regex process="(?i)LDAP://[^\s\"\']+" | regex process="(?i)(password|pwd|bindpassword|secret)\s*[=:]\s*\S{4,}"
Bulk download from Tchap homeserver to single endpoint (media/attachment exfil) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a single endpoint or account pulling abnormally large volumes from Tchap's media/attachment endpoints over a short window — the pattern matching the 13.5 GB attachment scrape advertised by 'Misère'. Tuned per-account so a normal heavy Tchap user does not generate the alert. Rationale: Article quantifies '13.5GB of documents and media files' — the only Tchap surface that ships media at that scale is the Matrix /_matrix/media/* endpoint family. Aggregating per (user, device, 15-min bucket) with thresholds on both call count and distinct media IDs captures sustained scraping while letting one-off heavy chats through. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/french-govt-says-tchap-breach-affected-over-73-000-accounts/ • https://spec.matrix.org/v1.10/client-server-api/#content-repository • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1567/
ATT&CKT1530 T1567 T1119
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DINUM-run archival or e-discovery export from Tchap
  • Compliance / records-management bots harvesting attachments per regulatory retention
  • New Tchap user catching up on a high-volume team room with months of media backfill
  • Forensics tool downloading attachments during an unrelated investigation
  • Tchap mobile-to-desktop migration re-syncing media cache
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("element.exe", "tchap.exe", "riot.exe") or MediaCalls > 5000
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm whether the account is sanctioned for bulk export (DINUM records team, e-discovery, compliance); inspect the source IP for ASN/geo anomalies; correlate against UC2 (room enumeration) on the same account — chained signal is high-confidence. 2) Contain: Coordinate with DINUM to block the offending Tchap account (consistent with their stated response); kill active sessions; block the egress IP at perimeter; preserve proxy and homeserver logs for CNIL notification timeline. 3) Hunt: Look for the same account previously enumerating rooms (UC2), downloading .ps1 / config files (UC3), and outbound transfers from the same source IP to file-sharing services (Mega, AnonFiles, Discord CDN) in the following 48 hours.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteUrl has "tchap.gouv.fr"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/_matrix/media", "/download", "/thumbnail")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize MediaCalls = count(),
            DistinctMedia = dcount(RemoteUrl),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            Clients = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 5)
            by bin(Timestamp, 15m), DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn
| where MediaCalls > 2000 and DistinctMedia > 500
| extend BurstSeconds = datetime_diff('second', LastSeen, FirstSeen)
| order by MediaCalls desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where Url has "tchap.gouv.fr"
| where Url has_any ("/_matrix/media", "/download", "/thumbnail")
| summarize MediaCalls = count(),
            DistinctMedia = dcount(Url),
            BytesIn = sum(HttpResponseBodyBytes),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by bin(TimeGenerated, 15m), SrcHostname, SrcUsername, SrcIpAddr
| where (MediaCalls > 2000 and DistinctMedia > 500) or BytesIn > 524288000
| order by BytesIn desc
source:(windows.sysmon OR proxy) (@DestinationHostname:(*tchap.gouv.fr OR *TCHAP.GOUV.FR) OR @http.url:(*tchap.gouv.fr* OR *TCHAP.GOUV.FR*)) (@http.url:(*\/_matrix\/media* OR *\/download* OR *\/thumbnail*))
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| join({#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/tchap\.gouv\.fr$/i | groupBy([aid, FirstIP4Record], function=count())}, field=[aid, RemoteAddressIP4], include=[DomainName])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, bin(@timestamp, 15m)], function=count(as=MediaConnections))
| MediaConnections > 2000
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true sum(Web.bytes_in) as bytesIn count as hits from datamodel=Web where Web.url like "%tchap.gouv.fr%" AND (Web.url like "%/_matrix/media/%" OR Web.url like "%/download/%" OR Web.url like "%/thumbnail/%") by _time span=15m Web.src Web.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where bytesIn > 524288000 OR hits > 2000
| tstats summariesonly=false sum(Web.bytes_in) as bytesIn count as hits from datamodel=Web where Web.url like "%tchap.gouv.fr%" AND (Web.url like "%/_matrix/media/%" OR Web.url like "%/download/%" OR Web.url like "%/thumbnail/%") by _time span=15m Web.src Web.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where bytesIn > 524288000 OR hits > 2000
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden

ShinyHunters Exploits Oracle PeopleSoft Zero-Day (CVE-2026-35273) to Breach Universities

The Hacker NewsBleepingComputer
2026-06-11 16 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The ShinyHunters extortion crew exploited an unpatched flaw in Oracle PeopleSoft to break into enterprise systems, steal data, and demand payment to keep it private. The campaign hit universities hardest. Google's Mandiant attributes it to the group it tracks as UNC6240, and dates the activity between May 27 and June 9. Oracle did not publish its advisory until June 10, so the bug was a

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] ShinyHunters Extortion Marker File 'README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT' Drop · [LLM] ShinyHunters '*_fanout.sh' SSH Credential-Spray Lateral Movement Script · [LLM] Outbound SMB (TCP/445) From PeopleSoft Host to Public IP — NetNTLM Coercion · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
PeopleSoft PSEMHUB Zero-Day Exploitation — POST to /PSEMHUB/hub or /PSIGW (CVE-2026-35273) AIExploitation Medium
Detects external POST requests to PeopleSoft Environment Management Hub or Integration Gateway endpoints — the exact entry points UNC6240 / ShinyHunters used to weaponise CVE-2026-35273 against PeopleTools 8.61 / 8.62. Mandiant's mitigation guidance explicitly calls out external POSTs to these two URL paths as the primary IoC. Rationale: Mandiant's published hunt guidance explicitly names POSTs to /PSEMHUB/hub and /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector as the exploitation surface; both URL paths are unique enough to PeopleSoft that any external POST is suspicious. Staging IPs 142.11.200.186-190, 108.174.202.99, and 176.120.22.24 are taken from the article.
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised internal vulnerability scanners (Tenable, Qualys, Rapid7) probing PSEMHUB
  • Penetration-test engagements with declared external IPs
  • Internal automation calling /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector for SOAP/REST integrations (should be on private IPs)
  • WAF/CDN health checks hitting wildcard URI prefixes
  • Mis-classified internal IP appearing as public due to NAT/proxy address bleed
Suppression filter
// Exclude declared scanner CIDRs
| where SourceIP !in ("<tenable-vm-cidr>","<qualys-cidr>","<rapid7-cidr>")
| where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Tenable","Qualys","Nessus","Rapid7")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull the full WAF/web log for the source IP — confirm POST body length, content-type, and any 200/500 response. Check Mandiant staging-IP list (142.11.200.186-190, 108.174.202.99, 176.120.22.24). 2) CONTAIN: block source IP at perimeter, then enforce Oracle's mitigation — disable PSEMHUB service (multi-server) or remove the PSEMHUB application (single-server), or at minimum block /PSEMHUB/* and /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector at the edge. WAF body inspection alone is bypassable per Mandiant. 3) HUNT: pivot to UC2 (.jsp webshell), UC3 (envmetadata XMLDecoder), UC4 (azurenetfiles.net) on the same host within 7 days before/after.
// Run against the proxy / WAF / WebLogic-fronting layer ingested into Sentinel
let StagingIps = dynamic(["142.11.200.186","142.11.200.187","142.11.200.188","142.11.200.189","142.11.200.190","108.174.202.99","176.120.22.24"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(CommonSecurityLog
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
 | where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
 | where RequestURL has_any ("/PSEMHUB/hub", "/PSEMHUB/", "/PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector")
 | where not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP)) or SourceIP in (StagingIps)
 | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, ReceivedBytes, SentBytes),
(W3CIISLog
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
 | where csMethod =~ "POST"
 | where csUriStem has_any ("/PSEMHUB/hub", "/PSEMHUB", "/PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector")
 | where not(ipv4_is_private(cIP)) or cIP in (StagingIps)
 | project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, scStatus, csBytes, sPort)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: PeopleSoft PSEMHUB Endpoint Exploitation (CVE-2026-35273)
id: a1b2c3d4-e5f6-4789-abcd-1111111111a1
description: External POST to PeopleSoft Environment Management Hub / Integration Gateway — UNC6240 (ShinyHunters) zero-day exploitation pattern
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/shinyhunters-exploits-oracle-peoplesoft.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/12
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.initial_access
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection_method:
    cs-method: POST
  selection_path:
    cs-uri-stem|contains:
      - /PSEMHUB/hub
      - /PSEMHUB/
      - /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector
  condition: selection_method and selection_path
level: high

(source:nginx OR source:apache.access OR source:iis OR source:cisco.asa OR source:paloalto.fw) @http.method:POST (@http.url_details.path:*/PSEMHUB/hub* OR @http.url_details.path:*/PSEMHUB/* OR @http.url_details.path:*/PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector*) -CIDR(@network.client.ip, 10.0.0.0/8) -CIDR(@network.client.ip, 172.16.0.0/12) -CIDR(@network.client.ip, 192.168.0.0/16)
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count, values(Web.url) as urls, values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents, values(Web.status) as statuses, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=POST AND (Web.url="*/PSEMHUB/hub*" OR Web.url="*/PSEMHUB/*" OR Web.url="*/PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector*") by Web.src, Web.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where NOT cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8", src) AND NOT cidrmatch("172.16.0.0/12", src) AND NOT cidrmatch("192.168.0.0/16", src) | convert ctime(firstTime), ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(Web.url) as urls, values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents, values(Web.status) as statuses, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=POST AND (Web.url="*/PSEMHUB/hub*" OR Web.url="*/PSEMHUB/*" OR Web.url="*/PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector*") by Web.src, Web.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where NOT cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8", src) AND NOT cidrmatch("172.16.0.0/12", src) AND NOT cidrmatch("192.168.0.0/16", src) | convert ctime(firstTime), ctime(lastTime)
Unexpected .jsp Webshell Written Under PSEMHUB.war Web Application Directory AIInstallation High
Hunts for newly-created or modified JSP files under the PSEMHUB.war web-app directory tree — Mandiant lists this as a direct post-exploitation IoC where attackers drop a webshell after the CVE-2026-35273 deserialization payload lands. PeopleSoft does not legitimately drop JSPs into PSEMHUB at runtime. Rationale: Article explicitly states 'Unexpected .jsp files under the PSEMHUB.war web application directory' as a Mandiant-published hunt indicator. PSEMHUB.war is a static deployment artifact — runtime JSP writes inside it are anomalous.
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised PeopleTools patch / PUM image deployment landing a new PSEMHUB.war
  • DBA-driven manual hotfix application that unzips a WAR into the exploded directory
  • Custom in-house PSEMHUB extension being deployed via Change Assistant
  • WebLogic JSP recompile temp files (usually under tmp/, not PSEMHUB.war root)
  • Backup/restore operations re-laying the WAR contents
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("changeassistant.exe","changeassistant","pum.sh","applyPatch.sh","unzip","tar")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("PUM","ChangeAssistant","applyPatch","PSPATCH")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: open the JSP — look for Runtime.exec, ProcessBuilder, base64-decoded payload, password gate (`request.getParameter("pwd")`), or Java reflection. Pull SHA256 and search VT. 2) CONTAIN: quarantine the file via MDE/Falcon, snapshot WebLogic stdout/stderr logs (the request that wrote it is usually visible there), and block /PSEMHUB/* at the perimeter. 3) HUNT: review WebLogic access logs for /PSEMHUB/<the_dropped_jsp_name>, hunt for outbound to azurenetfiles.net (UC4) and inbound from staging IPs 142.11.200.186-190 in the 24h preceding the file write.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has "PSEMHUB"
| where FileName endswith ".jsp" or FileName endswith ".jspx" or FileName endswith ".war"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, FileSize,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFilePath has "PSEMHUB"
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("jsp","jspx","war") or TargetFileName endswith_cs ".jsp" or TargetFileName endswith_cs ".jspx"

PeopleSoft XMLDecoder Persistence via envmetadata/data/environment XML Modification AIInstallation High
Detects modification or creation of XML files under the web doc root's envmetadata/data/environment path — Mandiant warns this path is abused for Java XMLDecoder persistence that fires on the next PeopleSoft restart, surviving patching of the original CVE-2026-35273 vector. Rationale: Article quotes Mandiant: 'Recently changed .xml files under the web doc root's envmetadata/data/environment, which can be abused for XMLDecoder persistence that fires on the next restart.' Path is highly specific to PeopleSoft and rarely written by legitimate runtime operations.
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1547 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Oracle PUM image apply re-laying environment XML files
  • Change Assistant patch run
  • Manual PeopleTools env reconfiguration by DBA (chronotrack against ticket)
  • Backup tool re-touching modification time without content change
  • WebLogic redeploy of the PSEMHUB application
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("changeassistant","applyPatch.sh","pum.sh","psadmin","psadmin.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("psadm2","psadmin","oracle","root") or InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("java","weblogic","sh","bash")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: diff the XML against the previous version (xmldiff or git blame on /etc-managed config). Look for `<java>`, `<object class="java.lang...">`, `<void method="exec">`, `Runtime.getRuntime` — those are XMLDecoder gadget chains. Compute SHA256 and compare across the PeopleSoft fleet. 2) CONTAIN: restore known-good XML from the PUM image, restart the WebLogic domain to flush any pre-loaded gadget. Quarantine the writing process if non-root/non-psadmin. 3) HUNT: review WebLogic access log for inbound exploit POST in the 60 min preceding the XML write (UC1), and pivot to outbound DNS for azurenetfiles.net (UC4) on the same host.

| where FileName endswith ".xml"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, FileSize,

| order by Timestamp desc

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

MeshCentral Agent C2 Beacon to azurenetfiles.net (UNC6240 / ShinyHunters) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects DNS resolution or network connection to azurenetfiles.net — the article-identified command-and-control domain used by the campaign's MeshCentral agents disguised as Microsoft Azure binaries. The lookalike domain mimics Azure NetApp Files; legitimate Azure infrastructure uses azurenetapp.net / azure.com, never this string. Rationale: Article identifies azurenetfiles.net as the campaign C2 and gives five Python SimpleHTTP staging IPs (142.11.200.186-190) plus two related infrastructure IPs. The domain is a typosquat of legitimate Azure NetApp Files and has no business use; any resolution is high-fidelity.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1219 T1036.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution Network_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal threat-intel sandbox detonating a sample that beacons (whitelist the sandbox host)
  • Security researcher manually browsing the IOC for triage from a hunt host
  • DNS recursive resolver caching upstream — the originating client is the real target
  • Misconfigured email-link rewriter pre-fetching the URL
  • Honeypot / canary that intentionally connects
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") or InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !has_any ("Google","Microsoft","Mozilla")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: identify the initiating process (look at InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName / ProductName — campaign disguises MeshCentral as 'Microsoft Azure' binaries; mismatch with the SHA256 reputation is the tell). Pull file from disk. 2) CONTAIN: sinkhole azurenetfiles.net at the resolver, block the 7 IOC IPs at the firewall, isolate the host via MDE/Falcon network containment. 3) HUNT: run UC1/UC2/UC3 on the same host backwards 7 days to find initial access and persistence; check ~/.bash_history for the campaign's shared command set; look for *_fanout.sh (UC6) and the README marker (UC5).

ShinyHunters Extortion Marker File 'README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT' Drop AIActions on Objectives High
Detects creation of the exact README marker file the article confirms ShinyHunters' fanout script drops into PeopleSoft directories on successfully compromised hosts. The filename is unique enough that any match is functionally a confirmed-breach signal. Rationale: Article verbatim: 'drops a marker file named README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT into PeopleSoft directories.' Filename is sufficiently unique that no allowlisting is needed — any hit is a confirmed-breach indicator.
ATT&CKT1485 T1657 T1491.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst placing the IoC sample for testing detection (allowlist sandbox host)
  • Tabletop / purple-team exercise dropping the marker intentionally (coordinate with red team)
  • Backup restore of an already-compromised filesystem image
  • Sample copy in malware analysis VM
  • Honeyfile placed deliberately as a canary
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: confirm filename match exactly (no typos — attackers may iterate). Pull the file content for the demand text and any threat-actor onion address. Snapshot the affected directory's modification times. 2) CONTAIN: assume host is compromised — network-isolate, do NOT wipe (preserve for IR), notify legal/comms within 1 hour given the extortion angle. 3) HUNT: enumerate every host writing the marker (likely fleet-wide via fanout.sh — pivot UC6). Cross-reference UC4 for C2, UC2/UC3 for the entry path. Notify Mandiant / FBI per article context — this is the same group hitting >100 orgs.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, FileSize,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ShinyHunters '*_fanout.sh' SSH Credential-Spray Lateral Movement Script AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts for execution, drop, or read of the fanout.sh script the article confirms ShinyHunters used for lateral movement: it sprays a hardcoded credential list over SSH against hosts pulled from /etc/hosts. The script is named with a victim prefix ([victim]_fanout.sh), so a wildcard match on *_fanout.sh is the right shape. Rationale: Article verbatim: 'The script, named [victim]_fanout.sh, spreads over SSH by spraying a hardcoded list of usernames and passwords against internal hosts pulled from /etc/hosts.' The naming convention is unique to this campaign.
ATT&CKT1110.003 T1021.004 T1570
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Red team / purple team replicating the campaign with a victim-named test script
  • IR/forensics team copying the captured fanout.sh sample to a sandbox for analysis
  • Detection-engineering team staging the IOC for rule testing
  • Threat-hunt notebooks importing the script for static analysis
  • Honeyfile placed as a tripwire
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("root") or ActingProcessName !has_any ("cp","scp","rsync","vim","less","cat","file")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: cat the script — confirm SSH spray pattern, extract the embedded username/password list, list of /etc/hosts targets, and any SHA256. Check if it has executed (auditd EXECVE / bash_history). 2) CONTAIN: isolate host, expire all SSH keys for accounts in the embedded list across the fleet, rotate any passwords that appear (assume compromised). Block outbound SSH from PeopleSoft hosts to non-approved internal subnets. 3) HUNT: pivot to every host in the embedded /etc/hosts target list — check for the README marker (UC5), inbound SSH success from the originating host, and outbound to azurenetfiles.net (UC4). Review .bash_history shared across the staging directory (the article notes a SHARED .bash_history across the attacker's five staging IPs — same command set should appear on victims).

Outbound SMB (TCP/445) From PeopleSoft Host to Public IP — NetNTLM Coercion AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects outbound SMB connections on TCP/445 from PeopleSoft hosts to public IP space — Mandiant warns the CVE-2026-35273 exploit chain may coerce the PeopleSoft service-account machine to authenticate to attacker-controlled SMB endpoints, leaking NetNTLM hashes that can be relayed or cracked. Legitimate PeopleSoft has no reason to SMB out to the internet. Rationale: Article verbatim: 'Outbound SMB traffic on port 445 from PeopleSoft hosts to external destinations, which the exploit chain may use to capture machine-account NetNTLM hashes.' Detection needs the inventory-join because outbound SMB to public IPs is benign from no host class but extremely anomalous from a PeopleSoft tier.
ATT&CKT1187 T1557.001 T1003.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Misconfigured PeopleSoft integration pulling a SharePoint Online file via SMB (rare — should use HTTPS)
  • Sysadmin testing connectivity to an external file share for migration planning
  • Azure Files / Azure NetApp Files connection from PeopleSoft (legitimate; uses *.file.core.windows.net IP space — allowlist)
  • Backup agent uploading to cloud storage that uses SMB endpoint
  • Misconfigured DNS causing internal SMB target to resolve to a public IP
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIP !endswith ".file.core.windows.net"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("azcopy.exe","backupagent.exe","vssvc.exe","system")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: identify the destination IP — is it Azure Files (40.x/52.x with file.core.windows.net rDNS) or unknown? Pull the initiating process and account; if SYSTEM/machine account, NetNTLM has likely already leaked. Capture pcap if possible. 2) CONTAIN: block outbound TCP/445 from PeopleSoft host subnets to public IPs at the firewall — there is no legitimate use case Mandiant accepts. Force rotation of the machine account password on the affected host. 3) HUNT: pivot to UC1 (PSEMHUB POST) on the same host — the coercion is triggered by the exploit. Check if the destination IP appears in any other host's traffic (campaign-wide IoC). Review domain controller authentication logs for NTLM relay attempts targeting privileged accounts.
// Populate via DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory or a managed watchlist of PeopleSoft hosts
let PeopleSoftHosts = DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where SoftwareVendor =~ "oracle" and (SoftwareName has "peoplesoft" or SoftwareName has "peopletools")
    | distinct DeviceId, DeviceName;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemotePort == 445 and Protocol =~ "Tcp"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where DeviceId in ((PeopleSoftHosts | project DeviceId))
     or DeviceName matches regex @"(?i)(peop|psemhub|psoft|psadmin|hcm|crm|fscm)"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("backupagent.exe","vssvc.exe","system")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
// Tag PeopleSoft hosts via watchlist or DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
let PeopleSoftHosts = DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where SoftwareVendor =~ "oracle" and (SoftwareName has "peoplesoft" or SoftwareName has "peopletools")
    | distinct DeviceName;
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DstPortNumber == 445 and NetworkProtocol =~ "TCP"
| where DstIpAddr !startswith "10." and DstIpAddr !startswith "192.168." and not(DstIpAddr matches regex @"^172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[0-1])\.") and not(ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr))
| where DvcHostname in (PeopleSoftHosts)
     or DvcHostname matches regex @"(?i)(peop|psemhub|psoft|psadmin|hcm|crm|fscm)"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkBytes, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
(source:windows.sysmon OR source:linux.auditd OR source:paloalto.fw OR source:cisco.asa) (@EventID:3 OR @network.destination.port:445) @network.destination.port:445 (@host:*peop* OR @host:*PSOFT* OR @host:*PSEMHUB* OR @host:*psadmin* OR @host:*hcm* OR @host:*fscm*) -CIDR(@network.destination.ip, 10.0.0.0/8) -CIDR(@network.destination.ip, 172.16.0.0/12) -CIDR(@network.destination.ip, 192.168.0.0/16) -CIDR(@network.destination.ip, 100.64.0.0/10)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemotePort=445 Protocol=6
| ComputerName=/(?i)(peop|psemhub|psoft|psadmin|hcm|fscm)/
| NOT cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("172.16.0.0/12", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("192.168.0.0/16", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("100.64.0.0/10", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4], function=count())
# log group: /aws/vpc/flowlogs
fields @timestamp, srcAddr, dstAddr, dstPort, bytes, action
| filter dstPort = 445
      and action = "ACCEPT"
      and not (dstAddr like /^10\./ or dstAddr like /^192\.168\./ or dstAddr like /^172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[0-1])\./ or dstAddr like /^100\.(6[4-9]|[7-9][0-9]|1[0-1][0-9]|12[0-7])\./)
| stats count(*) as conns, sum(bytes) as totalBytes by srcAddr, dstAddr
| sort conns desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)

            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-35273")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-35273")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — A tale of two eras
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Talos prevalent-malware IOC hit: Coinminer/Injector/Dropper hashes + VID001.exe lure · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Talos prevalent-malware IOC hit: Coinminer/Injector/Dropper hashes + VID001.exe lure AIInstallation High
Hunts for the four SHA256/MD5 hashes Talos published in the 2026-06-11 Threat Source newsletter as the most prevalent malware files in their telemetry that week (Win.Worm.Coinminer, W32.Injector, Win.Dropper.Miner), plus the example lure filename VID001.exe. Article-specific — these are concrete, freshly-curated reputation hits from a Tier-1 vendor's weekly telemetry, not a generic miner template. Rationale: Uses the four SHA256 hashes (9f1f11..., 96fa6a..., a31f22..., 9896a6...), four MD5 hashes (2915b3..., aac316..., 7bdbd1..., 38de5b...) and the lure filename VID001.exe published verbatim in the Talos newsletter as their weekly prevalent-malware roundup. Talos detection names (Win.Worm.Coinminer::1201, W32.Injector:Gen.21ie.1201, Win.Dropper.Miner::95.sbx.tg) provide secondary corroboration; the hashes are themselves Talos-authoritative IOCs so no external second source is required. Combines reviewer suggestions #1 (Coinminer/VID001.exe) and #2 (W32.Injector) into a single hash-IOC match since the article provides no behavioural detail beyond the hashes. Cross-checked against: • https://talosintelligence.com/talos_file_reputation?s=9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507 • https://talosintelligence.com/talos_file_reputation?s=96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974 • https://talosintelligence.com/talos_file_reputation?s=a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1496 T1055
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst workstation detonating these specific samples in a sandbox VM (filter on dedicated malware-lab device groups)
  • Red-team or purple-team exercise that seeded public Talos IOCs as known-bad payloads for control validation
  • Threat-intel ingestion pipeline (e.g. MISP/ThreatFox sync) writing the sample files into a quarantined research share but never executing them — generates DeviceFileEvents hits without process execution
  • AV/EDR engine itself quarantining the file and emitting a hash-tagged action event that downstream telemetry shippers re-log
  • Sample harvested by EDR scheduled scans of mounted forensic images (DFIR workstation reviewing a prior incident)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ (dynamic(["MALWARE-LAB-01","DFIR-WS-01","SANDBOX-DETONATE-01"])) and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","falcon-sensor.exe","CSFalconService.exe")
Response runbook
Triage: confirm the hit is on a real production endpoint (not a sandbox/DFIR/red-team device); pull the full process tree for the matching SHA256/MD5/VID001.exe execution, the parent process, and the originating file write to identify the delivery vector (browser download, email attachment, USB, SMB share). Contain: isolate the endpoint via Defender/Falcon network containment, block the SHA256 hashes via custom IOC indicator (Defender CIM / Falcon IOC Management), and quarantine any DeviceFileEvents copies still on disk. Hunt: pivot on the parent process and download URL/email to find other recipients that received the same lure but haven't executed yet; sweep DeviceNetworkEvents from infected hosts for mining-pool traffic (stratum+tcp://, common ports 3333/4444/5555/7777/14444) and other beaconing not blocked by network containment; check DeviceImageLoadEvents for unsigned DLLs loaded by the injector sample to map post-exploitation persistence.
let TalosHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507","96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974","a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91"]);
let TalosMd5 = dynamic(["2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f","aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9","7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376","38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98"]);
union
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where SHA256 in (TalosHashes) or MD5 in (TalosMd5) or FileName =~ "VID001.exe" or InitiatingProcessSHA256 in (TalosHashes) or InitiatingProcessMD5 in (TalosMd5)
  | project Timestamp, Source="Process", DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, MD5, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
),
( DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where SHA256 in (TalosHashes) or MD5 in (TalosMd5) or FileName =~ "VID001.exe"
  | project Timestamp, Source="FileWrite", DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, MD5, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
)
| order by Timestamp desc
let TalosSha256 = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507","96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974","a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91"]);
let TalosMd5 = dynamic(["2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f","aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9","7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376","38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98"]);
union isfuzzy=true
( SecurityEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where EventID == 4688
  | where FileHash in~ (TalosSha256) or FileHash in~ (TalosMd5) or NewProcessName endswith "\\VID001.exe"
  | project TimeGenerated, Source="4688", Computer, Account=SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, FileHash
),
( ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where SHA256 in~ (TalosSha256) or MD5 in~ (TalosMd5) or TargetProcessName endswith "\\VID001.exe"
  | project TimeGenerated, Source="ASIM", Computer=DvcHostname, Account=ActorUsername, NewProcessName=TargetProcessName, CommandLine=TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, FileHash=SHA256
),
( ImFileEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (TalosSha256) or TargetFileMD5 in~ (TalosMd5) or TargetFileName =~ "VID001.exe"
  | project TimeGenerated, Source="ASIM-FileWrite", Computer=DvcHostname, Account=ActorUsername, NewProcessName=ActingProcessName, CommandLine=ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName="", FileHash=TargetFileSHA256
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New Attacks Trick OpenClaw AI Agent Into Running Code and Leaking Secrets

The Hacker News
2026-06-11 15 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Two security teams have shown, in separate research published this week, that OpenClaw, the popular self-hosted AI agent, can be driven to run attacker-controlled code or hand over sensitive data through ordinary-looking inputs. Imperva buried instructions inside shared contacts, vCards, and location pins that the agent executed without the victim ever seeing them. Varonis built a test agent on
