Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] Vulnerable OpenClaw install (pre-2026.4.23) inventoried in the estate
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] OpenClaw agent process spawns LOLBin or interpreter (tool-use code execution) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] DNS or network egress to Imperva PoC infrastructure (imperva_artifactory.com) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] AI agent process reads credential stores then egresses to external destination · [LLM] OpenClaw outbound mail to first-time / external recipient (agent-phishing exfil) · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
DNS or network egress to Imperva PoC infrastructure (imperva_artifactory.com) AICommand & Control High
Hunts for any host resolving or connecting to the Imperva researcher-controlled domain used in the OpenClaw vCard / shared-contact prompt-injection PoC. Any production hit means an agent followed the embedded instruction and downloaded a payload. Rationale: Domain imperva_artifactory.com is the only article-cited IOC and is the literal server the Imperva PoC instructed the agent to fetch a script from. Any DNS / network hit is high fidelity. CloudWatch left empty: CloudTrail does not log host-level DNS or outbound HTTP and VPC Flow Logs do not carry hostnames — wrong telemetry surface for a domain-name pivot.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised internal red-team replaying the Imperva PoC in a lab
  • Security researchers reproducing the disclosure on a sandbox VM
  • Threat-intel ingestion service crawling the URL to label it
  • URL-rewriting mail gateway (e.g. Defender Safe Links / Proofpoint URL Defense) detonating an inbound link
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("defender.exe", "MsSense.exe", "smartscreen.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "SafeLinks"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the device is an OpenClaw / Pinchy-style host and pull the initiating process tree — was a python / node / runtime fetching the URL? Capture the script body downloaded. 2) Contain: isolate the host in MDE / Falcon, kill the agent runtime, revoke any cloud credentials or API tokens loaded into that agent's memory or env-vars. 3) Hunt: review the past 7d of inbound message-channel events (WhatsApp/Slack/Discord/Matrix/Teams/Zalo connectors) for contact / vCard / location objects whose name field contains angle brackets `<` `>` or the string `imperva_artifactory.com`; pivot on the agent's outbound mail / Slack / Discord for any secrets it may have already relayed.
let SuspectDomain = "imperva_artifactory.com";
union isfuzzy=true
  (DeviceNetworkEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
   | where RemoteUrl has SuspectDomain
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ReportId),
  (DeviceEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
   | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse" or ActionType == "DnsConnectionInspected"
   | where RemoteUrl has SuspectDomain or AdditionalFields has SuspectDomain
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, AdditionalFields, ReportId)
| order by Timestamp desc
let SuspectDomain = "imperva_artifactory.com";
union isfuzzy=true
  (DnsEvents
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
   | where Name has SuspectDomain
   | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, IPAddresses=Result),
  (ImDnsActivity
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
   | where DnsQuery has SuspectDomain
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsQueryTypeName, DnsResponseName),
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
   | where RequestURL has SuspectDomain or DestinationHostName has SuspectDomain
   | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DeviceAction)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OpenClaw agent process spawns LOLBin or interpreter (tool-use code execution) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for child processes spawned by the OpenClaw runtime (python/node) where the child is a shell, script interpreter, or download LOLBin — the on-host signature of the Imperva tool-use code execution attack where the agent followed an injected instruction to download and run a script. Rationale: Article names OpenClaw and the Varonis research clone Pinchy. The Imperva PoC concretely says the agent was told to 'download and run a script' — that materialises as the agent runtime (python/node) spawning curl/wget/powershell/bash. Pairing parent (agent) + child (LOLBin) avoids the bare-process-execution anti-pattern. CloudWatch left empty: this is on-host EDR telemetry, not AWS API telemetry.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.003 T1059.004 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate agent recipes invoking curl/git via a tool plugin
  • Developer running OpenClaw interactively and asking it to run a shell command
  • CI/CD job exercising agent integration tests that intentionally shell out
  • Agent self-update routine pulling a release via curl
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "--self-update" and ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("pytest", "unittest", "npm test")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull ProcessCommandLine for the child and the immediate parent — was the agent fed an inbound contact / vCard / location / email at the time? Capture the script body or URL. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the runtime, rotate every credential the agent has access to (mailbox tokens, AWS keys, SSH keys, channel-extension tokens for Slack/Discord/Matrix/Teams/Zalo). 3) Hunt: pivot on the parent agent process for the past 7 days for any other LOLBin spawns, any DNS to imperva_artifactory.com, and any outbound mail to first-time recipients — Varonis explicitly flagged 'first-time-send' as the Pinchy exfil signature.
let AgentParents = dynamic(["python.exe","python3","python","node.exe","node","openclaw.exe","openclaw","pinchy.exe","pinchy"]);
let SuspChildren = dynamic(["powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","bash.exe","wsl.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (AgentParents)
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("openclaw","OpenClaw","pinchy","Pinchy")
   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\openclaw\\","/openclaw/","\\pinchy\\","/pinchy/")
| where FileName in~ (SuspChildren)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, ReportId
| order by Timestamp desc
let AgentParents = dynamic(["python.exe","python3","python","node.exe","node","openclaw.exe","openclaw","pinchy.exe","pinchy"]);
let SuspChildren = dynamic(["powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","bash","sh","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (SecurityEvent
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
   | where EventID == 4688
   | extend ParentLeaf = tostring(split(ParentProcessName, "\\")[-1])
   | extend NewLeaf = tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1])
   | where ParentLeaf in~ (AgentParents) or ParentProcessName has_any ("openclaw","pinchy")
   | where NewLeaf in~ (SuspChildren)
   | where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
   | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine),
  (ImProcessCreate
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
   | extend ParentLeaf = tostring(split(ParentProcessName, iff(ParentProcessName has "\\", "\\", "/"))[-1])
   | extend ChildLeaf = tostring(split(TargetProcessName, iff(TargetProcessName has "\\", "\\", "/"))[-1])
   | where ParentLeaf in~ (AgentParents) or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("openclaw","pinchy")
   | where ChildLeaf in~ (SuspChildren)
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security OR linux.auditd) (@ParentImage:(*\python.exe OR *\python3.exe OR *\Python.exe OR *\node.exe OR *\Node.exe OR *\openclaw.exe OR *\OpenClaw.exe OR *\pinchy.exe OR *\Pinchy.exe) OR @ParentCommandLine:(*openclaw* OR *OpenClaw* OR *pinchy* OR *Pinchy*) OR @ParentImage:(*\openclaw\* OR */openclaw/* OR *\pinchy\* OR */pinchy/*)) AND @Image:(*\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\cmd.exe OR *\bash OR *\sh OR *\curl.exe OR *\wget.exe OR *\certutil.exe OR *\bitsadmin.exe OR *\mshta.exe OR *\wscript.exe OR *\cscript.exe OR *\rundll32.exe OR *\regsvr32.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (ParentBaseFileName=/^(python|python3|node|openclaw|pinchy)(\.exe)?$/i OR ParentImageFileName=/(\\|\/)(openclaw|pinchy)(\\|\/)/i OR ParentCommandLine=/(openclaw|pinchy)/i)
| ImageFileName=/(\\|\/)(powershell|pwsh|cmd|bash|sh|zsh|curl|wget|certutil|bitsadmin|mshta|wscript|cscript|rundll32|regsvr32)(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=[count(), min(@timestamp), max(@timestamp)])

AI agent process reads credential stores then egresses to external destination AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Varonis 'agent phishing' exfiltration pattern: an OpenClaw / Pinchy runtime reading credential files (.aws/credentials, .env, id_rsa, .ssh/config) within a short window of an outbound HTTP/SMTP send. Targets the article's documented outcome of AWS IAM keys, DB connection strings, and SSH credentials being forwarded in plaintext. Rationale: Varonis explicitly observed Pinchy 'forwarding mock AWS IAM access keys, database connection strings, and SSH credentials in plaintext' after a phishing email — the file paths above are the canonical homes for those three credential classes. Joining the credential read to a public-egress connection within 5m models the read-then-send signature. CloudWatch left empty: the read happens on the agent host, not in CloudTrail.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1005 T1041
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running OpenClaw locally with an agent recipe that legitimately calls AWS / SSH
  • Agent self-deployment routine reading its own .env config and then making API calls to a SaaS connector
  • Backup agent (Restic, Borg) collocated on the same host reading credentials
  • Configuration-drift / IaC tooling (Ansible, Terraform) running adjacent to the agent
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !has_any ("sts.amazonaws.com", "iam.amazonaws.com", "ec2.amazonaws.com") and RemoteIP !startswith "169.254."
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the agent's recent inbox / chat connector activity for inbound messages from outside addresses asking for credentials, exports, or 'urgent' access — Varonis's Dan-as-team-lead and weekly-QBR-export pretexts are the templates. 2) Contain: revoke every AWS access key, SSH key, DB credential, and SaaS token in the env-files the agent touched; rotate before notifying. 3) Hunt: enumerate all hosts running OpenClaw (any version below 2026.4.23 is also vulnerable to the Imperva vector); check Slack/Discord/Matrix/Teams/Zalo channel-extension allowlists for entries resolved by display name rather than stable ID — the InfoSec Write-ups static-analysis class of bug.
let AgentImages = dynamic(["python.exe","python3","python","node.exe","openclaw.exe","pinchy.exe"]);
let CredPaths = dynamic(["\\.aws\\credentials","/.aws/credentials","\\.env","/.env","\\.ssh\\id_rsa","/.ssh/id_rsa","\\.ssh\\config","/.ssh/config","\\.docker\\config.json","/.docker/config.json","\\.kube\\config","/.kube/config"]);
let CredReads = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType in ("FileOpened","FileCreated","FileModified")
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (AgentImages)
       or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\openclaw\\","/openclaw/","\\pinchy\\","/pinchy/")
    | where FolderPath has_any (CredPaths) or FileName in~ ("credentials",".env","id_rsa","id_ed25519")
    | project ReadTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessId, FolderPath, FileName;
let AgentEgress = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (AgentImages)
       or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\openclaw\\","/openclaw/","\\pinchy\\","/pinchy/")
    | where RemoteIPType == "Public"
    | project NetTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort;
CredReads
| join kind=inner (AgentEgress) on DeviceId
| where NetTime between (ReadTime .. ReadTime + 5m)
| project ReadTime, NetTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', NetTime, ReadTime), DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by ReadTime desc
let AgentImages = dynamic(["python.exe","python3","python","node.exe","openclaw.exe","pinchy.exe"]);
let CredPaths = dynamic(["\\.aws\\credentials","/.aws/credentials","\\.env","/.env","\\.ssh\\id_rsa","/.ssh/id_rsa","\\.ssh\\config","/.ssh/config","\\.kube\\config","/.kube/config"]);
let CredReads = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventType in ("FileAccessed","FileCreated","FileModified")
    | where ActingProcessName has_any (AgentImages)

let AgentEgress = ImNetworkSession

    | where DvcAction != "Deny"
    | where NetworkDirection == "Outbound"
    | project NetTime=TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url;
CredReads
| join kind=inner (AgentEgress) on DvcHostname
| where NetTime between (ReadTime .. ReadTime + 5m)
| project ReadTime, NetTime, DelaySec=datetime_diff('second', NetTime, ReadTime), DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url
| order by ReadTime desc

OpenClaw outbound mail to first-time / external recipient (agent-phishing exfil) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Implements the Varonis-recommended control: alert when an OpenClaw / Pinchy agent identity sends mail to a recipient address the org has not previously corresponded with. Targets the exfil shape observed in both Varonis simulations (mock AWS keys to outside Gmail; 247-customer export to a routine-sounding requester). Rationale: Varonis lays out four controls and 'no first-time sends to unfamiliar addresses without approval' is the primary mailflow gate. The two named pretexts (Dan-team-lead from outside Gmail; weekly QBR customer export) both materialise as outbound mail from the agent identity to a new external recipient with a credential or dataset attachment. Falcon/CloudWatch left empty: mailflow telemetry lives in M365/Workspace, not FDR or CloudTrail.
ATT&CKT1114.003 T1567 T1071.003
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate first-time customer contact via an agent-driven outreach campaign
  • Vendor onboarding email to a brand-new partner domain
  • Agent-generated meeting-invite to a new external contact
  • Help-desk auto-reply to a first-time inbound sender
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the message body and any attachments; check for AWS key prefixes (AKIA / ASIA), connection strings (postgres://, mongodb://, mysql://), and PEM headers. 2) Contain: quarantine the message, suspend the agent's mailbox sending, and revoke any credentials whose values appear in the body or attachments. 3) Hunt: look back 30 days for the requester address and any related thread that primed the agent — Varonis observed 'urgency beat the verify-sender rule once and routine beat it the second time', so check for either 'urgent' / 'production incident' language or 'weekly/QBR/customer export' phrasing in inbound mail to the agent.
let AgentSenders = dynamic(["openclaw@","pinchy@","agent@","agent-"]);
let Baseline = EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(60d) .. ago(1d))
    | where EmailDirection in ("Inbound","Outbound","Intra-org")
    | summarize by RecipientEmailAddress;
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where EmailDirection == "Outbound"
| where SenderFromAddress has_any (AgentSenders)
   or SenderDisplayName has_any ("openclaw","pinchy","OpenClaw","Pinchy")
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderDisplayName, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, AttachmentCount, UrlCount
| order by Timestamp desc
let AgentSenders = dynamic(["openclaw@","pinchy@","agent@","agent-"]);
let Baseline = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(60d) .. ago(1d))
    | where Operation in ("Send","SendAs","Receive")
    | mv-expand Recipients
    | extend Recip = tostring(Recipients)
    | summarize by Recip;
OfficeActivity

| where Operation in ("Send","SendAs")
| where Sender has_any (AgentSenders) or UserId has_any (AgentSenders)
| mv-expand Recipients
| extend Recip = tostring(Recipients)
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on Recip
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Sender, Recip, Subject, ItemAttachments, MessageId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable OpenClaw install (pre-2026.4.23) inventoried in the estate AIWeaponization High
Surfaces every host running OpenClaw at a version below 2026.4.23 — the patched release that moves contact / vCard / location label content out of the prompt body. Anything below this line is exploitable via the Imperva message-object prompt-injection vector. Rationale: Article explicitly states 'shipped a fix in version 2026.4.23' and tells defenders to update — so an inventory pivot on the version boundary is the cleanest detectable artefact. The version comparison logic encodes the boundary precisely (anything before 2026.4.23 is vulnerable).
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Lab / isolated VM intentionally pinned to vulnerable version for research
  • Air-gapped install awaiting a maintenance window
  • Inventory feed lag where a recently-upgraded host hasn't re-reported yet
  • Renamed binary / forked build that legitimately doesn't track the upstream version string
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each host, confirm OpenClaw is in active use vs dormant install — check ProcessRollup2 for recent execution. 2) Contain: schedule patch to 2026.4.23+ within the change window; for high-sensitivity hosts (mailbox-connected, AWS-credentialled), disable the message-channel extensions (Slack/Discord/Matrix/Teams/Zalo) until patched — the InfoSec Write-ups disclosure showed the same display-name-vs-stable-ID bug class across all five. 3) Hunt: pivot every pre-patch host through the LOLBin-child UC and the credential-read UC for the past 30 days to see if exploitation has already occurred.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName has "OpenClaw" or SoftwareVendor has "OpenClaw"
| extend Major = toint(extract(@"^(\d+)", 1, SoftwareVersion))
| extend Minor = toint(extract(@"^\d+\.(\d+)", 1, SoftwareVersion))
| extend Patch = toint(extract(@"^\d+\.\d+\.(\d+)", 1, SoftwareVersion))
| where Major < 2026
   or (Major == 2026 and Minor < 4)
   or (Major == 2026 and Minor == 4 and Patch < 23)
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion
| order by Timestamp desc

| where SoftwareName has "OpenClaw" or SoftwareVendor has "OpenClaw"
| extend Major = toint(extract(@"^(\d+)", 1, SoftwareVersion))
| extend Minor = toint(extract(@"^\d+\.(\d+)", 1, SoftwareVersion))
| extend Patch = toint(extract(@"^\d+\.\d+\.(\d+)", 1, SoftwareVersion))
| where Major < 2026
   or (Major == 2026 and Minor < 4)
   or (Major == 2026 and Minor == 4 and Patch < 23)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion
#event_simpleName=InstalledApplication
| (ApplicationName=/OpenClaw/i OR Vendor=/OpenClaw/i)
| ApplicationVersion=/^(202[0-5]\.|2026\.[0-3]\.|2026\.4\.(?:[0-9]|1[0-9]|2[0-2])$)/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ApplicationName, ApplicationVersion], function=count())

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent

| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",

   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")

The Hacker News

Security researcher Chaotic Eclipse (aka Nightmare-Eclipse and MSNightmare) has released a new Windows BitLocker bypass dubbed GreatXML, a day after they published an exploit for Microsoft Defender. "This was an accidental discovery, it took a total of 4 hours to find this," the researcher said in a post on Blogger. "If you ever attempted to use Windows Defender Offline Scan, you're

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution

GreatXML staging: unattend.xml + ReAgent.xml dropped to Recovery partition root AIWeaponization High
Hunts the core GreatXML pre-boot staging artifact: a process writing 'unattend.xml' to the root of the recovery partition and 'ReAgent.xml' under a 'Recovery\WindowsRE\' path on that same volume. Combination is the signature step that primes WinRE for an unrestricted BitLocker-volume shell after a Shift+Restart boot. Rationale: Article explicitly names the two staging files and the exact relative path 'Recovery/WindowsRE/ReAgent.xml' written to the recovery partition root. Requiring BOTH file writes on the same host within a short window collapses FPs from normal ReAgent.xml maintenance (Windows updates touch only ReAgent.xml, never paired with an unattend.xml on the recovery volume). Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-greatxml-exploit-bypasses-windows.html
ATT&CKT1542.005 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • MDT/SCCM-style OS provisioning workflows that stage unattend.xml on Recovery volume during imaging
  • OEM factory recovery image refresh that re-seeds Recovery\WindowsRE\ReAgent.xml during a Windows feature update
  • Acronis/Macrium Reflect recovery image creation writing ReAgent and unattend stubs
  • Sysprep cleanup tasks that legitimately drop unattend.xml in non-standard mount paths during golden image capture
Suppression filter
and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("dism.exe","sysprep.exe","setupact.exe","reagentc.exe","trustedinstaller.exe","sccm.exe","smsswd.exe","acronis_cloud.exe","reflect.exe")
| where not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("services.exe","wuauclt.exe","tiworker.exe") and InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "reagentc.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the initiating process tree on the host; confirm whether the writer is a known imaging tool (sccm.exe, dism.exe, sysprep.exe, acronis*.exe) or an interactive shell/PowerShell session. Check whether MpCmdRun.exe initiated a Defender Offline Scan in the prior 48h (GreatXML prerequisite). 2) Contain: if no provisioning workflow is in flight, isolate the device, disable WinRE via `reagentc /disable`, and force a TPM/PIN BitLocker recovery key rotation on that volume before the next reboot. 3) Hunt: pivot on the writing account across other hosts for the same paired-file write within 7d; review any Shift+Restart / WinRE boot events in Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-Boot/Operational. Escalate to IR if the host has high-value BitLocker-protected data.

reagentc.exe WinRE reconfiguration (setreimage / setosimage / boottore) AIInstallation High
Detects reagentc.exe being driven with flags that point WinRE at attacker-controlled images or force the next boot into the recovery environment. GreatXML requires a primed WinRE state so the planted XML pair is consumed on reboot, and operator-driven reagentc invocations outside patch/imaging workflows are the highest-fidelity precursor. Rationale: Article requires WinRE to be in a 'primed' (e.g., post offline-scan) state for the planted XML pair to be honoured. reagentc.exe is the only supported user-mode tool for /setreimage, /setosimage, and /boottore, and outside Windows servicing/imaging stacks these flags are almost never used legitimately - they directly stage the WinRE-side prerequisite GreatXML needs. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-greatxml-exploit-bypasses-windows.html • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/manufacture/desktop/reagentc-command-line-options
ATT&CKT1542.005 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT technician troubleshooting WinRE with `reagentc /setreimage` after a botched in-place upgrade
  • MDT/SCCM task sequence calling reagentc to re-point recovery image to a corporate WIM
  • OEM recovery refresh after a major Windows feature update
  • Help-desk-driven `reagentc /boottore` to capture user data ahead of a wipe-and-reload
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("sccm","smsswd","intune") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\CCM\", @"\MININT\", @"\Windows\Panther\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the operator account, parent process (interactive shell vs. SCCM/TI), and whether a change ticket exists for WinRE re-imaging. Check DeviceFileEvents on the same host for paired writes of unattend.xml + ReAgent.xml in the prior 30 minutes. 2) Contain: if no ticket, isolate the host before the next reboot - GreatXML triggers on WinRE entry. Cancel any pending boot-to-recovery via `reagentc /disable` then `reagentc /enable` once the WIM is verified. 3) Hunt: search 30-day reagentc.exe usage by the same account / cluster; correlate with MpCmdRun.exe `-OfflineScan` runs (article-cited prerequisite); review BitLocker key escrow for rotations matching these hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "reagentc.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/setreimage","/setosimage","/boottore"," boottore")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("tiworker.exe","trustedinstaller.exe","wuauclt.exe","setuphost.exe","sccm.exe","smsswd.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688

| where CommandLine has_any ("/setreimage", "/setosimage", "/boottore", " boottore")
| where not (ParentProcessName has_any ("TiWorker.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","wuauclt.exe","SetupHost.exe","sccm.exe","smsswd.exe"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"

| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Suspicious reagentc.exe WinRE Reconfiguration (GreatXML Precursor)
id: 1f8b6f0e-2b5a-4a8b-9e3c-7c6a1a44ad21
description: Detects reagentc.exe being invoked with flags that re-point WinRE at an attacker-controlled image or force-boot the next reboot into the recovery environment - the staging step described in the GreatXML BitLocker bypass.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-greatxml-exploit-bypasses-windows.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/12
tags:
  - attack.t1542.005
  - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_image:
    Image|endswith: '\reagentc.exe'
  selection_flags:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/setreimage'
      - '/setosimage'
      - '/boottore'
  filter_servicing:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\TiWorker.exe'
      - '\TrustedInstaller.exe'
      - '\SetupHost.exe'
      - '\wuauclt.exe'
  condition: selection_image and selection_flags and not filter_servicing
level: high
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*\\reagentc.exe OR *\\Reagentc.exe OR *\\REAGENTC.EXE) @CommandLine:(*\/setreimage* OR *\/setosimage* OR *\/boottore*) -@ParentImage:(*\\TiWorker.exe OR *\\TrustedInstaller.exe OR *\\wuauclt.exe OR *\\SetupHost.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\reagentc\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/(\/setreimage|\/setosimage|\/boottore)/i
| NOT (ParentBaseFileName=/^(TiWorker\.exe|TrustedInstaller\.exe|wuauclt\.exe|SetupHost\.exe)$/i)
| UserName!=/\$$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as process values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent values(Processes.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="reagentc.exe" AND (Processes.process="*/setreimage*" OR Processes.process="*/setosimage*" OR Processes.process="*/boottore*" OR Processes.process="* boottore*") by Processes.dest Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where NOT match(parent,"(?i)(TiWorker\.exe|TrustedInstaller\.exe|wuauclt\.exe|sccm.*\.exe)") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as process values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent values(Processes.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="reagentc.exe" AND (Processes.process="*/setreimage*" OR Processes.process="*/setosimage*" OR Processes.process="*/boottore*" OR Processes.process="* boottore*") by Processes.dest Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where NOT match(parent,"(?i)(TiWorker\.exe|TrustedInstaller\.exe|wuauclt\.exe|sccm.*\.exe)") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
Defender Offline Scan trigger (MpCmdRun -OfflineScan / BootSchedule) as GreatXML precursor AIWeaponization Medium
Article: 'If you ever attempted to use Windows Defender Offline Scan, you are automatically vulnerable to a BitLocker bypass.' Hunts hosts where MpCmdRun.exe scheduled or executed an offline scan, since this is the explicit precondition that primes WinRE for the GreatXML XML-drop attack. Rationale: The article calls out 'Defender Offline Scan ever initiated' as the necessary precondition for GreatXML, making MpCmdRun -OfflineScan / BootSchedule a high-value vulnerability inventory query. Joining against the unattend.xml/ReAgent.xml writes from UC1 lets analysts flag hosts that have both been primed AND staged. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-greatxml-exploit-bypasses-windows.html • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/threat-protection/microsoft-defender-antivirus/command-line-arguments-microsoft-defender-antivirus
ATT&CKT1542.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • End user clicking 'Microsoft Defender Offline scan' from Windows Security UI after a malware alert (entirely legitimate but creates the same precondition)
  • SOC IR playbook that mandates an offline scan after EDR detections
  • Vendor remediation scripts that schedule an offline scan as part of cleanup
  • Sysadmin verifying offline-scan functionality on a freshly imaged host
Response runbook
1) Triage: treat hits as an asset-inventory feed rather than an alert - tag each device 'GreatXML-vulnerable'. Cross-reference with UC1 results to find devices that are BOTH primed (Defender offline) AND staged (XML pair planted). 2) Contain: for staged+primed hosts, enforce BitLocker pre-boot PIN where missing and rotate recovery keys; consider compensating control of disabling WinRE on high-value endpoints (`reagentc /disable`). 3) Hunt: review 90-day MpCmdRun.exe history; build a watchlist of vulnerable hosts so future XML-write alerts on those devices auto-escalate to high severity.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "MpCmdRun.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-OfflineScan","BootSchedule","-Scan -ScheduleJob -RestartMachine")
| summarize OfflineScanCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            SampleCmd = any(ProcessCommandLine), SampleAccount = any(InitiatingProcessAccountName)
            by DeviceName, DeviceId
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName in~ ("unattend.xml","ReAgent.xml")
    | where FolderPath has_any (@"\Recovery\", @"\WindowsRE\", "HarddiskVolume")
    | summarize StagingArtifacts = make_set(FileName), StagingLastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceId
) on DeviceId
| extend Vulnerable = OfflineScanCount > 0, Staged = isnotempty(StagingArtifacts)
| project DeviceName, FirstSeen, LastSeen, OfflineScanCount, SampleAccount, SampleCmd, Vulnerable, Staged, StagingArtifacts, StagingLastSeen
| order by Staged desc, LastSeen desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\MpCmdRun.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("-OfflineScan", "BootSchedule", "-Scan -ScheduleJob -RestartMachine")
| summarize OfflineScanCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            SampleCmd = any(CommandLine), SampleAccount = any(AccountName)
            by Computer
| order by LastSeen desc

WinRE-initiated cmd.exe with BitLocker volume access (post-exploit shell) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the post-exploitation result described in the article: a shell spawned inside WinRE with unrestricted access to a normally BitLocker-protected volume. Pivots on cmd.exe / X:\WINDOWS\System32 parentage and subsequent file enumeration of the protected C: drive from a winload/winre-context process. Rationale: Article describes the end-state as 'a shell spawned with unrestricted access to the BitLocker volume' inside WinRE. Process telemetry from inside the WinRE ramdisk (always X:\) is extremely rare in normal operations and is the cleanest single-pivot tell that the exploit succeeded and the attacker is now operating against the protected C: drive. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-greatxml-exploit-bypasses-windows.html • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/manufacture/desktop/windows-recovery-environment--windows-re--technical-reference
ATT&CKT1006 T1542.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin running diskpart/manage-bde from WinRE during a legitimate BitLocker recovery
  • Helpdesk-driven Startup Repair flows that fall back to a WinRE cmd.exe
  • OEM recovery-image utilities that surface a recovery shell during break-fix
  • MDT/SCCM in-place upgrade rollback that boots into WinRE for cleanup
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("StartupRepair","BootRec","WinRESetup") and DeviceName has_any ("-IT-","-LAB-","-IMG-"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm via change/ticket records whether the host was knowingly booted to WinRE; pull DeviceFileEvents to enumerate which BitLocker-protected files were touched from the X:\ context. Look for any file writes outward to USB / removable media (potential exfil of the protected volume). 2) Contain: physically secure the device, force a TPM reset and BitLocker key rotation; if evidence of data access, treat as a confirmed BitLocker bypass and escalate to IR + DPO. 3) Hunt: 90-day sweep for the same X:\ process pattern fleet-wide; correlate with UC1/UC2/UC3 to find hosts that were primed, staged, then executed.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith @"X:\" or FolderPath startswith @"X:\"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","notepad.exe","manage-bde.exe","reagentc.exe","diskpart.exe","robocopy.exe","xcopy.exe")
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith @"X:\"
    | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
    | where FolderPath !startswith @"X:\"
    | summarize TouchedFiles = make_set(FolderPath, 25), FileCount = count() by DeviceId
) on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          TouchedFiles, FileCount
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName startswith @"X:\" or ParentProcessName startswith @"X:\"
| extend Bin = tostring(split(NewProcessName, @"\")[-1])
| where Bin in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","notepad.exe","manage-bde.exe","reagentc.exe","diskpart.exe","robocopy.exe","xcopy.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Process Execution from WinRE Volume (X:\) - GreatXML Post-Exploit Shell
id: e4a9f0d2-1b6b-4f2a-9e51-91c8a23c5d7e
description: Detects process creations where the image or parent image resolves to the WinRE ramdisk root (X:\). GreatXML lands the attacker in a cmd.exe inside WinRE with unrestricted access to the BitLocker-protected OS volume.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-greatxml-exploit-bypasses-windows.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/12
tags:
  - attack.t1542.005
  - attack.t1006
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    - Image|startswith: 'X:\'
    - ParentImage|startswith: 'X:\'
  filter_binary:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\notepad.exe'
      - '\manage-bde.exe'
      - '\reagentc.exe'
      - '\diskpart.exe'
      - '\robocopy.exe'
      - '\xcopy.exe'
  condition: selection and filter_binary
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:(X\:\\Windows\\System32\\* OR X\:\\WINDOWS\\System32\\* OR X\:\\Sources\\*) OR @ParentImage:(X\:\\Windows\\System32\\* OR X\:\\WINDOWS\\System32\\*)) @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\manage-bde.exe OR *\\reagentc.exe OR *\\diskpart.exe OR *\\robocopy.exe OR *\\xcopy.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (ImageFileName=/^X:\\/i OR ParentImageFileName=/^X:\\/i)
| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|notepad|manage-bde|reagentc|diskpart|robocopy|xcopy)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, ParentImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.parent_process_path) as parent_path from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_path="X:\\WINDOWS\\System32\\*" OR Processes.parent_process_path="X:\\WINDOWS\\System32\\*" OR Processes.process_path="X:\\Sources\\*") AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","notepad.exe","reagentc.exe","manage-bde.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.process_name Processes.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.parent_process_path) as parent_path from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_path="X:\\WINDOWS\\System32\\*" OR Processes.parent_process_path="X:\\WINDOWS\\System32\\*" OR Processes.process_path="X:\\Sources\\*") AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","notepad.exe","reagentc.exe","manage-bde.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.process_name Processes.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`

C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),

| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false

| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45585")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45585")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Webserver process writes PHP-executable file to public web-root or upload directory (CVE-2026-48062) AIInstallation High
Detects php-fpm, nginx, httpd, w3wp, caddy or the php interpreter creating .php / .phar / .phtml / .phps / .pht files under common public web roots (public, webroot, htdocs, www, uploads, public_html). The CodeIgniter4 ext_in bypass advisory explicitly warns of this landing-on-disk artefact when applications save with the original client filename via $file->move($path). Rationale: Anchors on the article's explicit conditions: 'save uploads using original client filename', 'store uploads in a web-accessible directory', 'allow PHP files to run from that directory'. The webserver-account UID writing a PHP-executable extension under /public is precisely the post-validation-bypass artefact. Filename-extension list (.php/.phar/.phtml/.phps/.pht) covers all PHP-handler-mapped extensions and matches the article's exact bypass example (shell.php).
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003 T1036.008
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Composer install / git pull during a legitimate deploy, when the webserver UID writes vendored .php files into public/
  • CMS plugin or theme installer writing .php under public/uploads/ via an in-app admin upload (WordPress, Drupal extension store)
  • Dev environment with hot-reload writing into the document root under the webserver UID
  • CodeIgniter4 cache writers writing PHP cache shards to writable/cache (filter via the writable/ prefix)
  • Imagick or thumbnailer wrappers that legitimately move processed assets into /public/uploads/thumbs/ — if any are .php-suffixed (rare)
Suppression filter
and not (FolderPath has_any (@"\writable\","/writable/",@"\vendor\","/vendor/",@"\.git\","/.git/")) and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("composer","git pull","git checkout","git clone","deploy")) and not (FileName startswith "index.php")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the file at FolderPath\FileName from a forensic copy — confirm presence of webshell strings (eval, system, base64_decode, assert, passthru) or polyglot GIF/JFIF magic followed by `<?php`. Pull the SHA256 to VirusTotal / internal sandbox. Identify the upload endpoint by tracing InitiatingProcessId backwards through DeviceProcessEvents. 2) Contain: quarantine the file (rename to .quarantine, chmod 000), block the source IP at WAF, and disable the affected CodeIgniter4 application or stop the webserver if active exploitation is ongoing. 3) Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessId for outbound NetworkConnect/DnsRequest from php-fpm/w3wp in the next 24h, look for additional .php drops on neighbour hosts behind the same load balancer, and confirm CodeIgniter4 version inventory against CVE-2026-48062 (UC 4 below).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-fpm.exe","php-cgi.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe","w3wp.exe","caddy.exe","php.exe")
| where FileName endswith ".php" or FileName endswith ".phar" or FileName endswith ".phtml" or FileName endswith ".phps" or FileName endswith ".pht"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\public\", @"\webroot\", @"\htdocs\", @"\www\", @"\uploads\", @"\public_html\", "/public/", "/webroot/", "/htdocs/", "/www/", "/uploads/", "/public_html/")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| where EventType =~ "FileCreated" or EventType =~ "FileRenamed" or EventType =~ "FileModified"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","php-cgi","httpd","nginx","w3wp","caddy","php.exe","php")

title: Webserver / PHP interpreter writes PHP-executable file to public web root (CVE-2026-48062)

  landing-on-disk artefact of the CodeIgniter4 ext_in upload-validation bypass (CVE-2026-48062) where
  a file named shell.php with GIF-like content passed `ext_in[avatar,gif]`.

Webserver / PHP interpreter spawns shell or LOLBin — post-upload RCE indicator AIExploitation High
Detects php-fpm, php-cgi, nginx, httpd, w3wp, caddy or php.exe directly spawning cmd/powershell/sh/bash or LOLBins (whoami, net, certutil, curl, wget, bitsadmin). The CodeIgniter4 ext_in bypass culminates in arbitrary code execution when the dropped PHP file is requested — this catches the resulting child process even when the on-disk artefact is missed. Rationale: Article's stated impact is 'arbitrary code execution' via the dropped PHP file being requested by the attacker. The PHP interpreter forking a shell or recon LOLBin is the classic post-webshell-execution shape and is extremely uncommon in production PHP stacks outside of imagemagick/ffmpeg wrappers, which can be excluded via cmdline. Parent-child pair is the high-fidelity signal — neither side alone qualifies.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.001 T1059.003 T1059.004 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • PHP applications using exec/system to call ImageMagick (convert), ffmpeg, or wkhtmltopdf — flag and allowlist by cmdline
  • WordPress / Drupal cron jobs shelling out to wp-cli or drush from php-fpm
  • Application-installed monitoring agents using whoami/hostname from PHP for diagnostics
  • Composer post-install / post-update scripts running during deploys
  • PHP-based queue workers (php-resque, Laravel Horizon) that legitimately spawn child processes for job isolation
Suppression filter
and not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("convert","ffmpeg","wkhtmltopdf","gs ","ghostscript","imagemagick","wp-cli","drush","artisan","composer")) and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("composer install","composer update","post-install","post-update"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full ProcessCommandLine and InitiatingProcessCommandLine — webshells frequently pass attacker input as the arg (e.g. 'cmd.exe /c whoami'). Pull the upstream PHP request from W3CIISLog/access logs around Timestamp ±5s using ProcessId correlation. 2) Contain: kill the PHP-FPM worker pool (systemctl restart php-fpm or iisreset), block source IP, and pull the on-disk PHP files written by that worker UID in the last 24h for analysis. 3) Hunt: enumerate further child processes from any php-fpm/w3wp in the org over the last 7d (DeviceProcessEvents | parent in PHP set), check for outbound C2 from those workers (DeviceNetworkEvents), and run UC1 to find the webshell artefact.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-fpm.exe","php-cgi.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe","w3wp.exe","caddy.exe","php.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh.exe","bash.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","reg.exe","hostname.exe","ipconfig.exe","systeminfo.exe","tasklist.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\\php-fpm.exe","\\php-cgi.exe","\\httpd.exe","\\nginx.exe","\\w3wp.exe","\\caddy.exe","\\php.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\curl.exe","\\wget.exe","\\whoami.exe","\\net.exe","\\net1.exe","\\reg.exe","\\hostname.exe","\\ipconfig.exe","\\systeminfo.exe","\\tasklist.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ProcessId, NewProcessId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HTTP multipart upload: image Content-Type with PHP/executable filename extension (CVE-2026-48062 exploit shape) AIDelivery High
Detects the exact bypass condition described in the advisory at the request layer: a multipart upload where the Content-Type header indicates an image (image/gif, image/png, image/jpeg) but the multipart filename ends in .php / .phtml / .phar / .phps. CodeIgniter4's pre-4.7.3 ext_in rule trusts the MIME-guessed extension and accepts the file. Requires WAF or application-level HTTP body parsing — IIS / Apache access logs alone do not expose multipart filenames. Rationale: Article names the exact rule: `ext_in[avatar,gif]` is bypassed by `shell.php` containing GIF-like content. The detectable signature at ingress is the multipart-part mismatch: declared Content-Type=image/* AND filename=*.php. WAF / app-tier HTTP logging is required (IIS/Apache plain access logs don't expose multipart filenames), so falcon_logscale_query and defender_kql are intentionally empty — FDR and Defender DeviceNetworkEvents don't carry decoded multipart part headers.
ATT&CKT1190 T1036.008
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal pentest / red-team running automated file-upload bypass tests against the same endpoint
  • Bug-bounty researcher submitting test payloads via a known WAF-allowed source IP
  • Misconfigured client uploading a .php file that the client incorrectly tagged as image/jpeg (rare, usually a browser-side bug)
  • WAF replay/debug traffic from QA environment that has been mirrored into the prod log stream
Suppression filter
and not (SourceIP in ("<pentest-egress-ip>","<bug-bounty-egress-ip>")) and not (UA has_any ("Burp","sqlmap","OWASP ZAP") and SourceIP startswith "10.")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full multipart body from the WAF and confirm whether the file was accepted by the upload endpoint (HTTP 200/302 vs 4xx). Identify the target CodeIgniter4 host(s) and the resolved file path on disk by tracing the SrcIpAddr to backend logs. 2) Contain: block SourceIP at the WAF, drop any uploaded artefact from disk after preserving a forensic copy, and verify CodeIgniter4 framework version >= 4.7.3 on the receiving app. 3) Hunt: search the prior 30d of WAF logs for the same SrcIpAddr against any upload endpoint org-wide, and pivot to UC1 / UC2 to see whether the dropped file was executed.
let UploadEndpoints = dynamic(["/upload","/avatar","/uploads","/file","/profile","/image","/photo","/picture"]);
let ImageMimes = dynamic(["image/gif","image/jpeg","image/jpg","image/png","image/webp","image/bmp","gif","jpeg","png","jpg","webp","bmp"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(
    CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
    | where RequestURL has_any (UploadEndpoints)
    | where FileType in~ (ImageMimes)
    | where FileName matches regex @"(?i)\.(php|phar|phtml|phps|pht)$"
    | project TimeGenerated, Vendor=DeviceVendor, SourceIP, DestHost=DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, FileName, FileType, UA=RequestClientApplication
),
(
    ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
    | where Url has_any (UploadEndpoints)
    | where FileMimeType in~ (ImageMimes)
    | where FileName matches regex @"(?i)\.(php|phar|phtml|phps|pht)$"
    | project TimeGenerated, Vendor=EventVendor, SourceIP=SrcIpAddr, DestHost=HttpHostName, RequestURL=Url, RequestMethod=HttpMethod, FileName, FileType=FileMimeType, UA=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: HTTP multipart upload — image MIME with PHP/executable filename extension (CVE-2026-48062)
id: 9f4e8b7c-2d6a-4c5e-8d1b-7a3c9e2f5d1a
description: |
  Multipart-form upload whose part declares an image MIME type (image/gif|png|jpeg|webp|bmp) but whose
  filename ends in a PHP-executable extension (.php/.phar/.phtml/.phps/.pht). This is the precise bypass
  condition for CodeIgniter4 CVE-2026-48062 where the ext_in rule trusts the MIME-guessed extension.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2gr4-ppc7-7mhx
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/12
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.t1036.008
logsource:
  category: webserver
  product: waf
detection:
  selection_method:
    cs-method: POST
  selection_mime:
    file-mime:
      - 'image/gif'
      - 'image/jpeg'
      - 'image/png'
      - 'image/webp'
      - 'image/bmp'
  selection_ext:
    filename|re|i: '\.(php|phar|phtml|phps|pht)$'
  condition: selection_method and selection_mime and selection_ext
falsepositives:
  - Security researcher / pentester running automated upload-validation tests against the same endpoint
  - Misconfigured CMS theme installer briefly carrying both image MIME and php filename for a polyglot widget
level: high
(source:apache.access OR source:nginx.access OR source:iis OR source:cloudflare OR source:imperva OR source:f5) @http.method:POST (@http.url_details.path:*upload* OR @http.url_details.path:*avatar* OR @http.url_details.path:*uploads* OR @http.url_details.path:*file* OR @http.url_details.path:*profile* OR @http.url_details.path:*image*) (@http.request.body.content_type:image\/* OR @http.headers.content_type:multipart\/form-data*) (@http.upload.filename:(*.php OR *.phar OR *.phtml OR *.phps OR *.pht OR *.PHP OR *.PHAR OR *.PHTML))
WEB
`waf` OR `cef` request_method=POST (uri_path="*/upload*" OR uri_path="*/avatar*" OR uri_path="*/uploads*" OR uri_path="*/file*" OR uri_path="*/profile*" OR uri_path="*/image*") (file_mime="image/gif" OR file_mime="image/jpeg" OR file_mime="image/png" OR file_mime="image/webp" OR file_mime="image/bmp" OR content_type="image/*")
| regex filename="(?i)\.(php|phar|phtml|phps|pht)$"
| stats count min(_time) as first_seen max(_time) as last_seen values(filename) as filenames values(file_mime) as mimes values(user_agent) as user_agents by src_ip dest http_host uri_path
| sort - last_seen
Vulnerable CodeIgniter4 framework inventory (CVE-2026-48062, < 4.7.3) AIReconnaissance High
Asset-state hunt: enumerates hosts where Defender TVM or Sentinel inventory reports composer:codeigniter4/framework at a version < 4.7.3, scoped by the CVE-2026-48062 advisory. Use this to drive patch deployment and prioritise application-layer monitoring for the run-time detections in UC1-UC3. Rationale: Pure inventory pivot using the CVE explicitly named in the advisory (CVE-2026-48062) and the affected package `composer:codeigniter4/framework` < 4.7.2. Sigma omitted because asset-state inventory is not a single-event-shape detection. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch omitted because composer-level framework inventory is not in their standard schemas — Defender TVM and Sentinel TVM are the canonical surfaces.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts with CodeIgniter4 vendored under a non-production path (CI runner image, archived backup) which is not actively served
  • Container hosts whose TVM scan reports the package inside a stopped image layer rather than a running container
  • Dev-only laptops with cloned codeigniter4/CodeIgniter4 git source for contributor work
  • Vendored CodeIgniter4 inside a parent application that ships its own patched fork (rare — verify with the app team)
Response runbook
1) Triage: cross-reference each DeviceName with the CMDB to identify owning team, application name, and exposure (internet-facing vs internal). Prioritise IsInternetFacing=true. 2) Contain: open a change ticket to upgrade composer:codeigniter4/framework to >= 4.7.3, and for any host that cannot patch within 72h apply the advisory's listed workarounds (move uploads outside webroot, use $file->store() or $file->move($path, $file->getRandomName()), disable PHP execution in upload dirs). 3) Hunt: enable UC1/UC2/UC3 alerting on the affected hosts and review the prior 30d of WAF logs against any upload endpoints those apps expose.

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48062")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48062")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
