Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

GoFlateLoader Uses Massive PE Overlay to Deliver Lumma, Vidar, and StealC Infostealers

Cyber Security News
2026-06-11 2 use cases 1 technique 2 kill-chain phases detected

A new malware loader called GoFlateLoader has been quietly spreading across the internet, and what makes it stand out is not how complex it is but how effective a simple trick has made it. Written in the Go programming language, this loader has one job: to decode and drop dangerous information-stealing programs onto a victim&#8217;s [&#8230;] The post GoFlateLoader Uses Massive PE Overlay to Deliver Lumma, Vidar, and StealC Infostealers appeared first on Cyber Security News .

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["b88c5744975d2abb447aecc6c090fee9f8580413f4612eecdc6ed1973e8a1739", "ed5ae7f36453c5a23e9868a5729d67e0549a11f6dea54f5f52d654a8f51d4902", "841c9297cb8a2e0ff89433d13c05bfc760eb2e98e251cb8fa785d2ad7cbac05f", "ece7c48eb411b24f26762ede83badb4a644c41d5777129381ac2541804d64fc2", "421ce2d2f49c23bbe9f60ef3b9cd38d7eb912ce02e56a61837656210069bd9e2", "121c2dc793b3873f75a29ec02241f94136de19c049382a50a50d0d5b99507073", "2415db5081cec9bfd14ad6da1a66169fd96f13a49010c319a73d1ed6fafd4efa", "d9917ade3b4c125a95b5d3e6343cde26145dfbf569bd7e2a843fd0c6fc8ddc28", "4cf6893756f441522b94b36f10e5de0e47aeed4743f95c51650746d1ecf97e3d", "8b89d6c9152d3aab97aadd515ecb69ca72654db2f25425759ba4b646853d737d", "90ce4ff9da23ac150da0a8e17930cab1e369aa349fdc1b65691b70369145664a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0b
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__HASH_LIST__` placeholder with article-specific SHA256
    values. Use a watchlist or external indicator file for management
    at scale.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    category: process_creation
    product: windows

        Hashes|contains:
            - 'SHA256=__HASH_PLACEHOLDER_REPLACE_ME__'

level: critical

The Gentlemen Ransomware Claims 478 Victims, Can Spread Like a Worm

The Hacker News
2026-06-11 12 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A new analysis of The Gentlemen operation has revealed that the financially motivated threat group initially operated as an affiliate responsible for conducting double extortion attacks, while leveraging resources from various ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) schemes like LockBit (aka Tenacious Mantis), Qilin (aka Pestilent Mantis), and Medusa (aka Venomous Mantis). Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("176.120.22.127") or RemoteUrl has_any ("")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["176.120.22.127"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic([""]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: network_connection
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
        DestinationHostname:
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    condition: selection_ip or selection_domain
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive IOC match
level: critical
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("176.120.22.127")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Miasma Phantom Gyp: ~157-byte binding.gyp file dropped in package root (npm install code-exec primitive) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Miasma and Hades Are Spreading Now: Detect Them on Developer Machines with Suspi
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Miasma/Hades: AI-agent or editor config file written outside the IDE (auto-exec on project open) · [LLM] Hades PyPI worm: Python interpreter spawns Bun runtime or downloads it from bun.sh/oven-sh · [LLM] Known Miasma/Hades payload SHA256 observed in file write or process execution · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Worm propagation signal: rapid serial npm publish or twine upload from a single developer host
Miasma/Hades: AI-agent or editor config file written outside the IDE (auto-exec on project open) AIInstallation High
Hunts the seven exact dotfile/dotfolder paths the StepSecurity write-up lists as Miasma/Hades auto-execute footholds (.vscode/tasks.json, .vscode/setup.mjs, .claude/setup.mjs, .claude/settings.json, .cursor/rules/setup.mdc, .gemini/settings.json, .github/setup.js). These files trigger code execution when the developer simply opens the folder in VS Code, Cursor, Claude Code or Gemini — no install, no lifecycle script. Suppresses writes initiated by the legitimate IDE binaries themselves so the surfaced events are dropper-style writes (git checkout, archive extraction, package post-install scripts, unsigned utilities). Rationale: Targets the exact seven auto-execute paths in Table 1 of the article. Cross-checked with Snyk and Semgrep write-ups (linked) confirming the Phantom Gyp/IDE-hook delivery primitives. Suppressing the IDE binaries themselves is the key FP cut — only the worm-style drop (npm/git/zip/python writing into another project's dotfolder) survives. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/node-gyp-supply-chain-compromise-self-propagating-npm-worm-binding-gyp/ • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/ironworm-and-new-miasma-worm-variant.html
ATT&CKT1546 T1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer cloning a legitimate repo template that already ships .vscode/tasks.json or .github/setup.js
  • yo / cookiecutter / create-react-app scaffolding tools writing IDE config on project bootstrap
  • Personal dotfiles bootstrapper (e.g. chezmoi, stow) seeding ~/.claude/settings.json
  • Anthropic Claude Code installer writing .claude/settings.json into the user profile path
  • Renovate/Dependabot bot committing a CI workflow file under .github/
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git.exe","npm.exe","node.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("clone","checkout","create-react-app","cookiecutter","yo ")) | where not (FolderPath startswith @"C:\Users\" and FolderPath endswith @"\.claude" and FileName =~ "settings.json" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "claude.exe")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — pull the file contents (Defender Live Response `getfile` or LogScale FileWritten WrittenBytes) and inspect: legitimate IDE configs are small, formatted JSON; Miasma/Hades drops carry obfuscated JS, fetch('https://bun.sh/...') strings, base64 blobs, or runOn:folderOpen with a shell payload. Check repo provenance — `git log -- <path>` will show the commit that introduced it. 2) CONTAIN — if malicious: isolate the host via Defender, revoke any cached npm/PyPI/GitHub/AWS tokens belonging to the user (the worm exfils to attacker GitHub repos), and quarantine the project tree. 3) HUNT — pivot on the same SHA256 across the fleet, check that user's recent `npm publish` / `twine upload` activity (UC5), and search GitHub audit logs for new SSH keys or repo creates from that account in the last 72h.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where (FolderPath has @"\.vscode" and FileName in~ ("tasks.json","setup.mjs"))
   or (FolderPath has @"\.claude" and FileName in~ ("setup.mjs","settings.json"))
   or (FolderPath has @"\.cursor\rules" and FileName =~ "setup.mdc")
   or (FolderPath has @"\.gemini" and FileName =~ "settings.json")
   or (FolderPath has @"\.github" and FileName =~ "setup.js")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Code.exe","Code - Insiders.exe","cursor.exe","claude.exe","gemini.exe","windsurf.exe","devenv.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where (TargetFilePath has @"\.vscode" and TargetFileName in~ ("tasks.json","setup.mjs"))
   or (TargetFilePath has @"\.claude" and TargetFileName in~ ("setup.mjs","settings.json"))
   or (TargetFilePath has @"\.cursor\rules" and TargetFileName =~ "setup.mdc")
   or (TargetFilePath has @"\.gemini" and TargetFileName =~ "settings.json")
   or (TargetFilePath has @"\.github" and TargetFileName =~ "setup.js")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("Code.exe","Code - Insiders.exe","cursor.exe","claude.exe","gemini.exe","windsurf.exe","devenv.exe")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Miasma/Hades AI-Agent or Editor Auto-Execute Config Dropped Outside IDE
id: 6f7f51bb-1d62-4bb5-8c92-4f4e3d2c1aa1
description: Detects creation of the AI-agent / editor configuration files that auto-execute on project open (.vscode/tasks.json runOn:folderOpen, .vscode/setup.mjs, .claude/setup.mjs SessionStart hook, .claude/settings.json, .cursor/rules/setup.mdc, .gemini/settings.json, .github/setup.js) by non-IDE processes — the Miasma/Hades worm foothold technique.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/miasma-and-hades-are-spreading-now-detect-them-on-developer-machines-with-suspicious-files
  - https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/
  - https://snyk.io/blog/node-gyp-supply-chain-compromise-self-propagating-npm-worm-binding-gyp/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/12
tags:

  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1059.007
logsource:

  product: windows
detection:
  selection_vscode_tasks:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\.vscode\tasks.json'
      - '\.vscode\setup.mjs'
  selection_claude:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\.claude\setup.mjs'
      - '\.claude\settings.json'
  selection_cursor:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\.cursor\rules\setup.mdc'

      - '\claude.exe'
      - '\gemini.exe'

  - Developer copying a project template that already contains these files
  - dotfiles repo bootstrapper writing personal IDE config

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:(*\\.vscode\\tasks.json OR *\\.vscode\\setup.mjs OR *\\.claude\\setup.mjs OR *\\.claude\\settings.json OR *\\.cursor\\rules\\setup.mdc OR *\\.gemini\\settings.json OR *\\.github\\setup.js)) -@Image:(*\\Code.exe OR *\\code.exe OR *\\Code\ -\ Insiders.exe OR *\\cursor.exe OR *\\Cursor.exe OR *\\claude.exe OR *\\Claude.exe OR *\\gemini.exe OR *\\Gemini.exe OR *\\devenv.exe OR *\\DEVENV.EXE)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\\\.((vscode\\(tasks\.json|setup\.mjs))|(claude\\(setup\.mjs|settings\.json))|(cursor\\rules\\setup\.mdc)|(gemini\\settings\.json)|(github\\setup\.js))$/i
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\\(Code|Code - Insiders|cursor|claude|gemini|windsurf|devenv)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.process_name) as process_name values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path values(Filesystem.file_hash) as file_hash from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*\\.vscode\\tasks.json" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.vscode\\setup.mjs" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.claude\\setup.mjs" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.claude\\settings.json" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.cursor\\rules\\setup.mdc" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.gemini\\settings.json" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.github\\setup.js") (Filesystem.action=created OR Filesystem.action=modified) NOT (Filesystem.process_name IN ("Code.exe","Code - Insiders.exe","cursor.exe","claude.exe","gemini.exe","windsurf.exe","devenv.exe")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | rename firstTime as first_time lastTime as last_time | convert ctime(first_time) ctime(last_time) | sort - last_time
Hades PyPI worm: Python interpreter spawns Bun runtime or downloads it from bun.sh/oven-sh AIInstallation High
Detects the Hades PyPI payload: an __init__.py / .pth hook fires on import, downloads a standalone Bun runtime, and executes a JavaScript credential stealer. Python interpreter as the parent of bun.exe (or as the parent of curl/wget/PowerShell fetching bun.sh, bun.com, or github.com/oven-sh/bun release tarballs) is a near-zero-baseline behaviour on normal developer machines. Rationale: Web search corroborated Hades downloads a standalone Bun runtime to run the JS stealer (Phoenix Security, Socket, Semgrep). Python.exe as parent of bun.exe is functionally zero-baseline on dev machines — Bun is a JS runtime, no reason for Python to launch it outside of this attack chain. Hash-blind, so survives the worm mutating its payload. Cross-checked against: • https://phoenix.security/miasma-azure-hades-pypi-supply-chain-worm-2026/ • https://socprime.com/active-threats/miasma-supply-chain-attack-spreads-through-the-phantom-gyp-worm/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/ironworm-and-new-miasma-worm-variant.html
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1105 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Polyglot developer running a Python helper that intentionally bootstraps a Bun-based JS test suite
  • CI agent (GitHub Actions self-hosted runner) on a dev workstation that uses a Python setup-step to install Bun
  • DevOps tooling like uv/poetry plugin invoking Bun via os.system for npm-mirror parity testing
  • Education / tutorial scripts that demonstrate cross-runtime tooling
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.py","conftest.py","poetry","uv ","tox") and ProcessCommandLine has "bun.sh/install" and AccountName !endswith "$" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","bash.exe"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — capture the Python parent's full command line and the Python virtualenv path; identify the imported package via `pip show` / `__init__.py` on disk and look for the obfuscated one-liner the article describes. Capture Bun binary SHA256 and any subsequent network egress from bun.exe. 2) CONTAIN — kill the bun.exe and Python process trees, isolate the host, revoke npm/GitHub/AWS/GCP/Azure/Vault/Kubernetes tokens (the documented exfil targets), and yank any cached PyPI token from ~/.pypirc / keyring. 3) HUNT — pivot on the offending PyPI package name across the fleet (`pip list`), check the StepSecurity Hades package list and ensmallen-family packages, and search Bun network egress for attacker-controlled GitHub repos used for token exfiltration.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python3.exe","python3.11.exe","python3.12.exe","python3.13.exe")
| where FileName =~ "bun.exe"
   or (FileName in~ ("curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bitsadmin.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("bun.sh","bun.com/install","oven-sh/bun","bun-windows-","bun-linux-","bun-darwin-"))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentImage=InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildImage=FolderPath, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python3.exe","python3.11.exe","python3.12.exe","python3.13.exe")
| where TargetProcessName =~ "bun.exe"
   or (TargetProcessName in~ ("curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bitsadmin.exe") and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("bun.sh","bun.com/install","oven-sh/bun","bun-windows-","bun-linux-","bun-darwin-"))
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Miasma Phantom Gyp: ~157-byte binding.gyp file dropped in package root (npm install code-exec primitive) AIExploitation High
Hunts the Phantom Gyp execution primitive: Miasma ships a 157-byte binding.gyp file that triggers code execution during the native-build phase of npm install, bypassing preinstall/postinstall script scanners entirely. Legitimate binding.gyp files for native node modules are several KB; a tiny binding.gyp landing inside a project tree (and especially being modified by git/npm/archive extraction rather than a developer editor) is the worm's tell. Rationale: The article specifies the binding.gyp is 157 bytes (size predicate <400 gives slack for variant builds). Cross-checked with StepSecurity v1 binding.gyp write-up, Snyk node-gyp supply-chain post, Semgrep Miasma v2 analysis — all converge on the same primitive. Excluding node-gyp's own bundled scaffold is the cleanest baseline cut. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://snyk.io/blog/node-gyp-supply-chain-compromise-self-propagating-npm-worm-binding-gyp/ • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1027.013
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • node-addon developer hand-writing a minimal binding.gyp during initial project setup
  • Generator tools like node-addon-api or cmake-js scaffolding a small starter binding.gyp
  • Test fixtures in node-gyp's own test suite (filtered by the node_modules path exclusion)
  • Educational tutorials reproducing 'hello world' native module examples
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "Code.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-addon","cmake-js","node-gyp configure")) | where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git.exe","7z.exe","tar.exe") and FolderPath has @"\node_modules\")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — pull the binding.gyp contents (Live Response getfile or LogScale FileWritten payload). A legitimate stub references `'targets': [{'target_name': '<name>', 'sources': ['*.cc']}]`; Miasma's variant invokes Python actions / shell commands or pulls a remote payload at build time. Cross-check the SHA256 against the article's five hashes. 2) CONTAIN — if malicious, isolate the host, kill any in-flight node-gyp/python.exe descendants, revoke the user's npm publishing token (npm token revoke), and prevent the package from being pushed onward. 3) HUNT — pivot on the package directory name across the fleet, check npm registry audit logs for new versions published from the user's account, and search the StepSecurity Miasma compromised-package list to identify the entry point.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName =~ "binding.gyp"
| where FileSize < 400
| where FolderPath !has @"\node_modules\node-gyp\"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName =~ "binding.gyp"
| where TargetFileSize < 400
| where TargetFilePath !has @"\node_modules\node-gyp\"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSize, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Known Miasma/Hades payload SHA256 observed in file write or process execution AIInstallation Medium
Direct IOC hit on the five SHA256 hashes the StepSecurity research team published for the Miasma and Hades campaigns. Matches across file writes (worm payload dropped to disk) and process execution (payload run). Hash-based detections are short-lived against a mutating worm but offer high-fidelity catches while the IOCs are still fresh. Rationale: Hashes are from the pre-extracted IOC list in the article. StepSecurity is the originating research source (acknowledged in JFrog and Semgrep follow-ups) so we ship as hunting-grade IOCs; rate them critical because hash collisions are nil and the worm is actively spreading at publish time. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-miasma-redhat-cloud-services/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal malware-analysis sandbox detonating a known sample
  • Threat-intel team copying the sample to a quarantine share for IR
  • Researcher running the sample against an EDR in a lab tenant
  • Backup software replicating quarantined files between tiers
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !startswith "sandbox-" | where DeviceName !startswith "malware-lab-" | where AccountName !in~ ("ir-analyst","threat-intel-svc")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — confirm the hit is on a production developer workstation, not a sandbox / lab host (check DeviceInfo tags). Pull the full process tree and file lineage; note which npm or PyPI package surfaced the payload. 2) CONTAIN — isolate the host immediately, revoke every credential cached on the box (npm, PyPI, GitHub, AWS, GCP, Azure, Vault, Kubernetes — per the documented worm targets), invalidate any in-flight package publish from the user's accounts, and ban the SHA256 fleet-wide via Defender custom indicators. 3) HUNT — search the last 30 days for other devices that touched the same package versions or downloaded artefacts from the same npm/PyPI registry path; pivot on the username for parallel publishing-token theft.

Worm propagation signal: rapid serial npm publish or twine upload from a single developer host AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the Miasma/Hades self-replication step: once the worm reads an npm or PyPI publishing token from process memory or ~/.npmrc / ~/.pypirc, it republishes infected versions of every package that token can publish. Multiple distinct package publishes from one host in a short window (the article reports ~57 npm packages and 286 versions republished in under two hours; 73 Microsoft Azure GitHub repos in two minutes) is a high-fidelity behavioural signal that survives any payload mutation. Rationale: Article: '57 npm packages across more than 286 malicious versions in a rolling campaign that lasted under two hours' and '73 repositories in under two minutes'. Cross-checked with Phoenix Security and Semgrep posts confirming the worm self-propagates by republishing every package the stolen token can reach. Threshold ≥3 distinct publishes in 30m on one host is well above typical legitimate publish cadence (devs cut a release, not a burst). Cross-checked against: • https://phoenix.security/miasma-azure-hades-pypi-supply-chain-worm-2026/ • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/ • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-miasma-redhat-cloud-services/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1552.001 T1567
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Monorepo release tooling (Lerna, Nx, Changesets, semantic-release) publishing many packages in one release
  • Developer cutting a coordinated multi-package SDK release manually
  • CI runner that happens to be a developer's own workstation publishing build artefacts
  • First-time publish of a freshly forked package set after maintainer handoff
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("lerna publish","nx release","changesets/cli","semantic-release","pnpm publish -r")) | where not (DeviceName startswith "build-" or DeviceName startswith "ci-runner-")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — list the packages just published and the npm/PyPI accounts they used (Defender's process command lines hold both). Compare the package set to the developer's normal portfolio — if they suddenly published packages they don't own, treat as confirmed worm. 2) CONTAIN — revoke the user's npm and PyPI publishing tokens immediately (npm token revoke / pypi.org account → 2FA tokens), yank the malicious versions (npm unpublish --force / pypi delete-release with the registry), and isolate the host. Notify downstream consumers of the affected packages. 3) HUNT — pull the user's IDE/terminal history and shell of recent project opens, look for Phantom Gyp binding.gyp (UC3) or Bun-from-Python (UC2) precursors in the prior 24h, and search the GitHub audit log for new SSH keys / personal-access tokens created from the user's account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where (FileName =~ "npm.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has " publish")
     or (FileName in~ ("twine.exe","twine") and ProcessCommandLine has "upload")
     or (FileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe") and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)twine\s+upload")
     or (FileName =~ "node.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm-cli.js publish","npm publish"))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize PublishCount = count(),
            DistinctCmds = dcount(ProcessCommandLine),
            SampleCmds = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 10),
            Parents = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 5),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
            by DeviceName, AccountName, bin(Timestamp, 30m)
| where PublishCount >= 3 and DistinctCmds >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where (TargetProcessName =~ "npm.exe" and TargetProcessCommandLine has " publish")
     or (TargetProcessName in~ ("twine.exe","twine") and TargetProcessCommandLine has "upload")
     or (TargetProcessName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe") and TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)twine\s+upload")
     or (TargetProcessName =~ "node.exe" and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm-cli.js publish","npm publish"))
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| summarize PublishCount = count(),
            DistinctCmds = dcount(TargetProcessCommandLine),
            SampleCmds = make_set(TargetProcessCommandLine, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |

    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966") or SHA1 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966") or MD5 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966") or SHA1 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966") or MD5 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GitHub has announced a major security-focused update to the Node Package Manager (npm), introducing breaking changes in the upcoming npm v12 release to reduce software supply chain attack risks significantly. The update, expected in July 2026, will turn off automatic execution of installation scripts by default, one of the most commonly abused mechanisms in malicious [&#8230;] The post GitHub to Automate Disable npm Script Installs to Block Supply Chain Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News .

Bun runtime install spawned by npm/node during package install (Shai-Hulud 2.0 signature) AIInstallation High
Detects npm, npx or node spawning the Bun runtime installer or executing the Shai-Hulud setup scripts (setup_bun.js / bun_environment.js) during package install. The article specifically calls out Shai-Hulud and Mini-Shai-Hulud installing the Bun runtime during preinstall as their distinguishing trait — Bun has no business appearing as a child of npm in normal dev workflows. Rationale: Datadog Security Labs and Unit 42 both document setup_bun.js / bun_environment.js as the Shai-Hulud 2.0 preinstall payload that installs Bun before stealing secrets. Bun spawned by npm/node is anomalous in normal dev workflows; the four string anchors (bun.sh/install, setup_bun.js, bun_environment.js, install.bun.sh) are direct campaign artefacts, not generic Bun usage. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/shai-hulud-the-novel-self-replicating-worm-infecting-hundreds-of-npm-packages • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/shai-hulud-v2-poses-risk-npm-supply-chain
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1195.002 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer manually installing Bun runtime via an npm-distributed wrapper such as `npm i -g bun` on a known dev workstation
  • CI runner with an intentional Bun build step that calls into node first
  • An internal tool that wraps Bun behind an npm script for cross-platform parity
  • A node-based installer for a Bun-using framework (e.g. Elysia/Hono starter)
Suppression filter
| where not(DeviceName has_any ("build-runner-","ci-") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "npm i -g bun")
Response runbook
1) Triage — pull the full `InitiatingProcessCommandLine` and the script body. If it references setup_bun.js or bun_environment.js, treat as confirmed Shai-Hulud and skip to step 2. Otherwise check the host inventory for a dev profile and confirm with the user that Bun install was intentional. 2) Contain — isolate the host via Defender LiveResponse, revoke the user's npm publish token, GitHub PAT, AWS keys and SSH keys, and quarantine the host's `~/.bun/`, `node_modules/` and `~/.truffler-cache/`. 3) Hunt — search the same window for `trufflehog` execution, outbound to `api.github.com/user/repos` from node/npm, and any newly-created public GitHub repos under the user's account with the description containing 'Shai-Hulud' or 'Sha1-Hulud'.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","npm.cmd","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","npm.cmd","npx.exe")
| where FileName =~ "bun.exe"
     or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("bun.sh/install","setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js","install.bun.sh",".bun/bin/bun")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.exe","npm.cmd","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
   or ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.exe","npm.cmd","npx.exe")
| where TargetProcessName endswith "bun.exe"
   or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("bun.sh/install","setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js","install.bun.sh",".bun/bin/bun")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Bun runtime install spawned by npm/node (Shai-Hulud signature)

description: Detects npm/node/npx spawning the Bun runtime installer or executing Shai-Hulud setup scripts (setup_bun.js / bun_environment.js) — the distinguishing signature of the Shai-Hulud and Mini-Shai-Hulud npm worms.
references:

  - https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/

TruffleHog secret scanner execution from .truffler-cache (Shai-Hulud credential harvest) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects execution of the TruffleHog binary out of the `~/.truffler-cache/` path used by Shai-Hulud 2.0 to cache the downloaded scanner, or any TruffleHog launch parented by node/npm/bun. The article calls out Shai-Hulud running TruffleHog to scrape secrets after install; this catches the actual credential-access step. Rationale: Datadog Security Labs documents `~/.truffler-cache/` as the explicit cache path Shai-Hulud uses for the downloaded TruffleHog binary, and the article names TruffleHog as the secret-scraping tool. A security tool of this kind has no business launching from npm install context on a dev endpoint — pairing the binary name with an npm/node/bun parent removes legitimate auditing use (which runs from CI tooling under runner SIDs, not interactive npm). Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.upwind.io/feed/shai-hulud-2-npm-supply-chain-worm-attack • https://safedep.io/shai-hulud-second-coming-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security engineer running TruffleHog interactively from a terminal that happens to have an npm process upstream
  • CI-runner workflow that uses TruffleHog as a pre-publish secret check (would normally run under a runner service account, not interactive user)
  • Developer testing a TruffleHog integration locally during onboarding
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessAccountName has_any ("sec-runner","trivy-svc","gh-actions-runner") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("runner.exe","Runner.Worker.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage — confirm the user did not knowingly launch TruffleHog; pull the `ProcessCommandLine` and look for `filesystem /` against the home directory (the Shai-Hulud invocation). 2) Contain — isolate the host, rotate every credential that lived in the user's `~/.aws/`, `~/.ssh/`, `~/.npmrc`, `~/.docker/config.json`, `~/.config/gh/`, browser keystores, and any cloud CLI session caches. Revoke the user's npm publish token and GitHub PAT immediately. 3) Hunt — pivot on `aid`/`DeviceId` for a `bun.exe` spawn shortly before, outbound to `api.github.com` from node/npm, and check the user's GitHub account for newly-created public repos with descriptions containing 'Shai-Hulud' / 'Sha1-Hulud: The Second Coming'.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "trufflehog" or FileName =~ "trufflehog.exe"
   or FolderPath has ".truffler-cache"
   or ProcessCommandLine has ".truffler-cache"
   or ProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog filesystem"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","npx.exe","bun.exe","sh","bash","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","npx.exe","bun.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName has "trufflehog"
   or TargetProcessCommandLine has ".truffler-cache"
   or TargetProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog filesystem"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.exe","npx.exe","bun.exe","bash","sh","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe")
   or ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.exe","npx.exe","bun.exe")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

npm/node spawning git or gh to create/push public GitHub repo (Nx s1ngularity & Shai-Hulud exfil) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects node, npm, or bun launching git, gh, or curl with arguments that create a new GitHub repository or push to `api.github.com/user/repos` — the exfiltration channel used by both Nx s1ngularity (`telemetry.js` → public repos of harvested tokens) and Shai-Hulud (public repos described as 'Sha1-Hulud: The Second Coming'). A package install legitimately does not create GitHub repos. Rationale: The article explicitly names public-GitHub-repo exfiltration as the channel for Nx s1ngularity (2025-08) and Shai-Hulud (2025-11); Datadog Security Labs confirms the 'Sha1-Hulud: The Second Coming' repo-description marker. Tying `api.github.com/user/repos` / `gh repo create` to an npm/node/bun parent collapses the FP space to roughly zero — package installs don't legitimately create GitHub repos. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.reversinglabs.com/blog/new-shai-hulud-worm-spreads-what-to-know
ATT&CKT1567.001 T1567 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer running `gh repo create` from a terminal where they recently invoked npm (parent-chain accidental match if shell process tree is short)
  • Internal scaffold/CLI that automates GitHub repo creation as part of `npm init` style flows
  • CI bot legitimately mirroring a repo via `git push --mirror` from a node-based pipeline runner
  • Open-source contributor using a node-based codemod that fans out PRs
Suppression filter
| where not(AccountName has "github-actions" or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("runner.exe","Runner.Worker.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage — pull the exact `ProcessCommandLine` and any environment variables; the Shai-Hulud markers are conclusive on their own. Check the user's GitHub account for new public repos created in the last 24h. 2) Contain — isolate the host, revoke the user's GitHub PAT and SSH key, force-delete the freshly-created public repos and audit which credentials were posted there for rotation, revoke npm publish token. 3) Hunt — sweep the org for the same SHA256 child binary across other hosts and look for the precursor TruffleHog + Bun execution chain on the same `aid`/`DeviceId`. Pull AAD/Okta sign-ins for the user from new geolocations in the last 7 days.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","npx.exe","bun.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","npx.exe","bun.exe")

node-gyp rebuild spawning unexpected non-build child process (binding.gyp implicit execution path) AIInstallation Medium
Detects the implicit `node-gyp rebuild` invoked when a package ships a `binding.gyp`, spawning a child that isn't a normal native-build toolchain process. The article calls this out as a stealth execution path: a package can have a spotless `package.json` and still execute code through the implicit gyp rebuild. Legit gyp rebuilds spawn Python, MSBuild, cl.exe, link.exe — anything else is suspect. Rationale: The article calls out `binding.gyp` and the implicit `node-gyp rebuild` as the 'spotless package.json' execution path that v12 closes off. Legitimate gyp rebuilds spawn a narrow set of C/C++ build tools; an anti-join against that allowlist catches deviation cheaply. References Aikido's own research write-up they link from the article on this specific path. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/npm-v12-block-postinstall
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1195.002 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A native-build package whose gyp invokes a custom helper executable outside the standard toolchain (e.g. SWIG, protoc, prebuild-install)
  • Developer machine with a non-standard Python wrapper (pyenv shim) that surfaces as an unusual binary name
  • CI runner caching gyp output via 7z.exe or tar.exe invoked from a custom gyp action
  • Cross-compilation toolchains that include clang.exe / mingw32-make.exe not in the allowlist
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("prebuild-install","swig","protoc","node-pre-gyp"))
Response runbook
1) Triage — capture the SHA256 of the child binary and look it up in VT and Aikido Intel; pull the offending package name from `InitiatingProcessCommandLine` (the gyp invocation includes the package path under `node_modules`). 2) Contain — block the package version in your internal registry / Verdaccio cache, and on the affected host quarantine `node_modules/<pkg>/build/` and the child binary. 3) Hunt — search org-wide for the same package directory hitting other hosts, and add the package name to the npm v12 deny-list for future installs.
let GypBuildChildren = dynamic(["python.exe","python3.exe","py.exe","msbuild.exe","cl.exe","link.exe","cmd.exe","conhost.exe","cscript.exe","node.exe","make.exe","nmake.exe","nasm.exe","ml64.exe","rc.exe","mt.exe","gyp.exe","where.exe","reg.exe","git.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp rebuild","node-gyp configure","node-gyp build","\\node-gyp\\bin\\node-gyp.js"))
     or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node-gyp.exe"
| where FileName !in~ (GypBuildChildren)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

     or ActingProcessName has "node-gyp.exe"
