| tstats `summariesonly` count as Successes, values(Authentication.user) as Users, values(Authentication.dest) as Appliances from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success Authentication.app IN ("fortigate","fortios","ssl-vpn","fortigate-admin") by Authentication.src, _time span=30m | `drop_dm_object_name("Authentication")` | join type=inner Authentication.src [ | tstats `summariesonly` count as Failures from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=failure Authentication.app IN ("fortigate","fortios","ssl-vpn","fortigate-admin") by Authentication.src, _time span=30m | `drop_dm_object_name("Authentication")` | where Failures >= 20 ] | where Successes >= 1 | sort - _time
| tstats summariesonly=false count as Successes, values(Authentication.user) as Users, values(Authentication.dest) as Appliances from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success Authentication.app IN ("fortigate","fortios","ssl-vpn","fortigate-admin") by Authentication.src, _time span=30m | `drop_dm_object_name("Authentication")` | join type=inner Authentication.src [ | tstats summariesonly=false count as Failures from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=failure Authentication.app IN ("fortigate","fortios","ssl-vpn","fortigate-admin") by Authentication.src, _time span=30m | `drop_dm_object_name("Authentication")` | where Failures >= 20 ] | where Successes >= 1 | sort - _time
Sub-second cadence burst of FortiGate post-auth CLI/API commands (MCP autonomous execution) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the execution phase of the MCP campaign on a freshly-compromised FortiGate: an authenticated session issues a burst of CLI/API commands at sub-second cadence — a rate no human admin can produce. The article's distinguishing feature vs traditional FortiGate compromise is that the post-auth tooling ran autonomously through an MCP server, not a human at a terminal, so the temporal fingerprint becomes the detection. Rationale: Article: "a custom MCP server running offensive tools autonomously" — the autonomous brain is what differentiates this campaign from a hands-on-keyboard FortiGate compromise. The temporal fingerprint (sub-second cadence of CLI/config-change events under one session) is the cleanest article-specific pivot. Uses CommonSecurityLog with DeviceExternalID for appliance identification (the previous DeviceName usage was schema-invalid). Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
ATT&CKT1059 T1106 T1078
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated FortiGate config backup / compliance tool (FortiManager, Tufin, AlgoSec) running a scheduled pull
  • Zero-touch provisioning script applying a baseline to a newly-onboarded appliance
  • FortiManager pushing a policy package across many appliances simultaneously
  • FortiAnalyzer or NOC dashboard polling 'diagnose' / 'get system' status at high frequency
  • Authorised BAS / red-team automation exercising the management plane
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<fortimanager-ip>","<fortianalyzer-ip>","<noc-poller-cidr>"]))
| where SourceUserName !in~ ("fortimanager","backup-svc","compliance-svc")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull the SourceUserName and SourceIP — is it a known FortiManager/orchestration system, or a SSL-VPN/admin login that should never drive config changes? Cross-reference with the initial-access UC: if this user authenticated 0–60 minutes earlier from a hosting ASN after a spray, escalate immediately. Step 2 (contain): kill the active admin/CLI session, force-disable the user, snapshot the running and startup configs and diff against the last known-good. Step 3 (hunt): walk the SampleCmds set for added admins, new local-in policies, SSL-VPN portal edits, or new port-forwards/VIPs; pivot to the C2 UC for outbound HTTPS from the appliance and to any newly-created admin accounts being reused on other appliances in the fleet.
// FortiGate CLI/API audit does not ship to Defender XDR — canonical detection is in Sentinel via CommonSecurityLog. Endpoint-side proxy: a single user's account driving sub-second remote operations against many internal hosts can be approximated via DeviceLogonEvents fan-out.
DeviceLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where ActionType == "LogonSuccess"
| where LogonType in ("Network","RemoteInteractive")
| summarize Logons = count(), Targets = dcount(DeviceId)
            by AccountName, RemoteIP, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where Logons > 30 and Targets > 10
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where DeviceProduct has_any ("FortiGate","Fortigate","FortiOS")
| where Activity has_any ("execute","config","diagnose","get system","cli","api call","edit","set","unset")
     or DeviceEventClassID has_any ("cfg-","cli-","event-system")
| summarize CmdCount = count(),
            DistinctCmds = dcount(Activity),
            SampleCmds = make_set(Activity, 25),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by ApplianceID = DeviceExternalID, SourceUserName, SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 10s)
| where CmdCount > 20                                  // 20 distinct CLI/config ops in 10s
| extend RateCmdsPerSec = todouble(CmdCount) / 10.0
| where RateCmdsPerSec > 2                             // > 2 ops/sec is super-human cadence
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:(fortinet OR fortigate OR syslog) @DeviceVendor:Fortinet (@Activity:(execute OR config OR diagnose OR "get system" OR edit OR set))
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as CmdCount, values(All_Changes.command) as Commands, min(_time) as FirstSeen, max(_time) as LastSeen from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.vendor_product IN ("FortiGate","FortiOS") All_Changes.action IN ("executed","modified","created","deleted") by All_Changes.user, All_Changes.src, All_Changes.dest, _time span=10s | `drop_dm_object_name("All_Changes")` | where CmdCount > 20 | eval RateCmdsPerSec = CmdCount / 10.0 | where RateCmdsPerSec > 2 | sort - _time
| tstats summariesonly=false count as CmdCount, values(All_Changes.command) as Commands, min(_time) as FirstSeen, max(_time) as LastSeen from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.vendor_product IN ("FortiGate","FortiOS") All_Changes.action IN ("executed","modified","created","deleted") by All_Changes.user, All_Changes.src, All_Changes.dest, _time span=10s | `drop_dm_object_name("All_Changes")` | where CmdCount > 20 | eval RateCmdsPerSec = CmdCount / 10.0 | where RateCmdsPerSec > 2 | sort - _time
Network appliance / jump host originating outbound HTTPS to LLM-API or MCP endpoints AICommand & Control Medium
Catches the C2 channel of the autonomous MCP campaign: edge appliances and jump hosts should never originate outbound traffic to Anthropic / OpenAI / Bedrock or to unknown JSON-RPC endpoints, but the article describes a custom MCP server brokering tasks between the LLM and the compromised fleet. Surfaces first-seen outbound to LLM-API FQDNs from devices in the network-infrastructure tier. Rationale: Kill-chain reconstruction explicitly calls out "Outbound HTTPS/JSON-RPC from network appliances or jump hosts to LLM-API or MCP-style endpoints" as the C2 fingerprint for this campaign, and the article frames the MCP server as the "orchestration brain" between the LLM and the compromised fleet. Edge devices originating AI-API traffic is a near-zero-baseline behaviour, so first-seen alone is high-signal. Cross-checked against: • https://modelcontextprotocol.io/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102.002 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised AI-assistant pilot deployed onto a bastion / jump host for ops automation
  • Vendor support tool on a network appliance that legitimately calls an LLM (e.g. Fortinet FortiAI, Palo Alto Precision AI)
  • Misclassified asset tag — a developer workstation incorrectly tagged as 'jumphost' calling api.openai.com for normal IDE use
  • Outbound proxy is a CDN-edge IP that also fronts the LLM endpoint, producing false-positive SNI matches
  • Security tool (BAS, scanner) running its own LLM-assisted analysis from a tagged DMZ host
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ (dynamic(["<approved-ai-pilot-host>","<bas-platform-host>"]))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): identify the source asset and confirm its role — is it a FortiGate, F5, jump host, or actually a misclassified user box? Pull the full DNS / SNI history for the asset in the last 7d and any auth events from the appliance UI immediately before the outbound. Step 2 (contain): if the asset is an edge appliance or bastion, block egress to the LLM FQDNs at the proxy/firewall and snapshot the device for forensics; do not reboot — MCP/agent state may live only in memory. Step 3 (hunt): pivot to the FortiGate auth UCs to find the matching initial-access event for the appliance, then sweep the fleet for the same outbound destinations from other devices in the infra tier; check for newly-created admin accounts whose creation timestamp falls within the C2 window.
let LLMHosts = dynamic([
    "api.anthropic.com","claude.ai",
    "api.openai.com","chat.openai.com",
    "bedrock-runtime","generativelanguage.googleapis.com",
    "api.mistral.ai","api.deepseek.com","api.x.ai"
]);
DeviceInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where DeviceCategory in~ ("NetworkDevice","Server")
   or DeviceType in~ ("NetworkDevice","Firewall","Router")
   or RegistryDeviceTag has_any ("jumphost","bastion","edge","dmz")
| summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId
| project DeviceId, DeviceName, DeviceCategory, RegistryDeviceTag
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
    | where RemotePort in (443, 8443)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any (LLMHosts)
       or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("mcp","model-context-protocol","jsonrpc")
) on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceCategory, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let LLMHosts = dynamic([
    "api.anthropic.com","claude.ai",
    "api.openai.com","chat.openai.com",
    "bedrock-runtime","generativelanguage.googleapis.com",
    "api.mistral.ai","api.deepseek.com","api.x.ai"
]);
let InfraSrcIPs = DeviceInfo
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where DeviceCategory in~ ("NetworkDevice","Server")
        or DeviceType in~ ("NetworkDevice","Firewall","Router")
        or RegistryDeviceTag has_any ("jumphost","bastion","edge","dmz")
    | summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by DeviceId
    | mv-expand PublicIP
    | project PublicIP = tostring(PublicIP);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceAction !~ "deny"
| where DestinationPort in (443, 8443)
| where (DestinationHostName has_any (LLMHosts) or RequestURL has_any (LLMHosts) or DestinationDnsDomain has_any (LLMHosts))
| join kind=inner (InfraSrcIPs) on $left.SourceIP == $right.PublicIP
| project TimeGenerated, ApplianceID = DeviceExternalID, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationDnsDomain, RequestURL, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(Web.url) as URLs, values(Web.user) as Users, min(_time) as FirstSeen from datamodel=Web where Web.dest IN ("api.anthropic.com","api.openai.com","bedrock-runtime.*.amazonaws.com","generativelanguage.googleapis.com","api.mistral.ai","api.deepseek.com") by Web.src, Web.dest, host | `drop_dm_object_name("Web")` | lookup network_infra_assets src OUTPUT asset_tier | where asset_tier IN ("edge-appliance","jump-host","firewall","vpn-gateway") | sort - FirstSeen

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

OceanLotus Hits Vietnam Investors With SPECTRALVIPER in FireAnt Attack

The Hacker News
2026-06-11 16 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The Vietnam-aligned threat actor known as OceanLotus has been attributed to two distinct campaigns that targeted domestic entities and stock investors with a backdoor known as SPECTRALVIPER. The campaigns involve a prolonged cyber espionage operation aimed at a Vietnamese infrastructure and transport construction corporation between mid-2024 and February 2026, as well as a supply chain attack

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] FireAnt Metakit supply-chain update — Metakit.exe pulls malicious setup.exe from metakit.fireant.vn · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Public-facing MSSQL exploitation — sqlservr.exe spawning cmd/powershell to drop SPECTRALVIPER · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — OceanLotus Hits Vietnam Investors With SPECTRALVIPER in FireAnt Attack
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] DtlCrashCatch.dll DLL side-load — rogue DLL loaded by signed FireAnt binary · [LLM] SPECTRALVIPER injection into OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe · [LLM] SPECTRALVIPER known-hash sweep — ESET-published SHA1 IOCs · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] SPECTRALVIPER C2 beaconing — financemachinelearning.com / gatewayrvcenter.com and IOC IPs · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
FireAnt Metakit supply-chain update — Metakit.exe pulls malicious setup.exe from metakit.fireant.vn AIDelivery High
Hunts the FireAnt Metakit auto-update channel abuse where the legitimate Metakit.exe fetched a tampered setup.exe from metakit.fireant[.]vn/Software/version.xml between Oct 2025 and Mar 2026. The update URL lacked signature validation, so any setup.exe pulled from that path during that window should be triaged as a supply-chain dropper. Rationale: Article names metakit.fireant[.]vn/Software/version.xml as the abused update URL and Metakit.exe as the parent that executed the malicious setup.exe without signature validation. Cross-checked OceanLotus tradecraft against MITRE G0050 page and ESET's prior SPECTRALVIPER reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0050/ • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/elastic-charms-spectralviper
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Metakit update rolled out before Oct 2025 retained in long-tail telemetry
  • Internal IT mirroring fireant update server for offline distribution
  • Penetration test simulating supply-chain abuse
  • Re-imaging script that bundles Metakit and chains the original update
  • Forensic replays of historical Metakit installs in a sandbox
Suppression filter
| where Timestamp between (datetime(2025-10-02) .. datetime(2026-03-09)) or SHA1 in ("865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D","B0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D205D6194","48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918BB028E947","511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39FB","8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B00037")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the SHA1/SHA256 of the dropped setup.exe and compare to the article IOC hashes (865A1739..., B0FEA981..., 48FEBB91...). Check whether the host belongs to a Vietnamese stock-trading user persona. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the device via Defender Live Response, block metakit.fireant.vn/Software/* at the proxy, and quarantine setup.exe + any DtlCrashCatch.dll. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the dropped setup.exe hash across the fleet, search for outbound connections to financemachinelearning.com / gatewayrvcenter.com, and check for OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe anomalies (UC #3).
let SuspectHosts = DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("metakit.fireant.vn/Software/version.xml","metakit.fireant.vn/Software/setup.exe") or RemoteUrl has_any ("financemachinelearning.com","gatewayrvcenter.com")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "Metakit.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "Metakit.exe"
| where FileName =~ "setup.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| union SuspectHosts
| order by Timestamp desc
let Net = ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has_any ("metakit.fireant.vn/Software/version.xml","metakit.fireant.vn/Software/setup.exe") or HttpHostName has_any ("financemachinelearning.com","gatewayrvcenter.com")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpHostName;
let Proc = SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\Metakit.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\setup.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName;
union isfuzzy=true Net, Proc
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: FireAnt Metakit Malicious Auto-Update Download
id: 9c8a14a2-7b3f-4d8e-9c1a-1f8e5d4b7a02
description: Detects Metakit.exe fetching the unsigned setup.exe auto-update used in the OceanLotus FireAnt supply-chain attack (Oct 2025-Mar 2026).
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/oceanlotus-hits-vietnam-investors-with.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/12
tags:

  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.initial_access
logsource:

  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\Metakit.exe'
    Image|endswith: '\setup.exe'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\Metakit.exe OR *\\metakit.exe) @Image:(*\\setup.exe OR *\\Setup.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^metakit\.exe$/i ImageFileName=/\\setup\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest in ("metakit.fireant.vn","financemachinelearning.com","gatewayrvcenter.com") OR All_Traffic.url="*metakit.fireant.vn/Software/version.xml*" OR All_Traffic.url="*metakit.fireant.vn/Software/setup.exe*" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.url All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest in ("metakit.fireant.vn","financemachinelearning.com","gatewayrvcenter.com") OR All_Traffic.url="*metakit.fireant.vn/Software/version.xml*" OR All_Traffic.url="*metakit.fireant.vn/Software/setup.exe*" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.url All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
DtlCrashCatch.dll DLL side-load — rogue DLL loaded by signed FireAnt binary AIInstallation High
Hunts the SPECTRALVIPER side-loading chain in which a legitimate signed binary loads the rogue DtlCrashCatch.dll from the same working directory. The DLL name is unique to this OceanLotus chain and not a known Windows component, so any image load or file write of that name is high-fidelity. Rationale: Article names DtlCrashCatch.dll as the rogue side-loaded DLL — not a real Windows / Dell / DTL component, so any presence is suspicious. Cross-referenced against MITRE T1574.002 and Elastic Labs' original SPECTRALVIPER write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/elastic-charms-spectralviper • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/002/
ATT&CKT1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis sandbox detonating the sample for research
  • Forensic acquisition copying the DLL off a compromised host
  • Threat-hunting team intentionally seeding the IOC for purple-team drills
  • Backup imaging of a known-infected host
  • Vendor-shared sample placed in a quarantine share
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Hash the DLL and compare against article SHA1s. Identify the loading process — anything other than the original FireAnt binary suggests a variant chain. Step 2 (contain): Quarantine the DLL and the host, block child C2 IPs/domains at the perimeter, capture memory of the loading process before kill. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep for the same SHA1/256 across the fleet and pivot on the loading binary's folder path — OceanLotus typically drops the legit signed loader and the rogue DLL into the same writeable directory.
let Files = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where FileName =~ "DtlCrashCatch.dll"
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, FolderPath, SHA1, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
let Loads = DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where FileName =~ "DtlCrashCatch.dll"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Windows\\System32\\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Windows\\SysWOW64\\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
union isfuzzy=true Files, Loads
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "DtlCrashCatch.dll"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA1, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SPECTRALVIPER DtlCrashCatch.dll Side-Load Artifact
id: a7f3e62d-1b94-4a8c-b8f2-2c3d6e7f0b13
description: Detects file write or image load of DtlCrashCatch.dll, the rogue side-loaded DLL used by OceanLotus to launch SPECTRALVIPER via the FireAnt supply-chain attack.
references:

  - https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/elastic-charms-spectralviper

tags:

  - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:

  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ImageLoaded|endswith: '\DtlCrashCatch.dll'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon (@EventID:7 OR @EventID:11) (@TargetFilename:(*\\DtlCrashCatch.dll OR *\\dtlcrashcatch.dll) OR @ImageLoaded:(*\\DtlCrashCatch.dll OR *\\dtlcrashcatch.dll))
(#event_simpleName=FileWritten OR #event_simpleName=ClassifiedModuleLoad) TargetFileName=/\\DtlCrashCatch\.dll$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName, SHA256HashData], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="DtlCrashCatch.dll" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_hash Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="DtlCrashCatch.dll" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_hash Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
SPECTRALVIPER injection into OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe AIInstallation Medium
Hunts SPECTRALVIPER's specific injection trick where the loader hollows / injects shellcode into OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe so the backdoor runs under a benign signed Microsoft binary. Detection focuses on OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe initiating outbound connections to non-Microsoft destinations or being spawned by an unusual parent. Rationale: Article explicitly states the rogue DtlCrashCatch.dll injects itself into OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe to trigger SPECTRALVIPER and the backdoor then beacons out — so OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe making non-Microsoft egress is the canonical hunt pivot. Cross-checked with Elastic Labs prior SPECTRALVIPER analysis. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/elastic-charms-spectralviper • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1055/012/
ATT&CKT1055.012 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • OneDrive consumer sync hitting CDN edges outside the curated allow-list
  • Personal OneDrive accounts on corporate hosts hitting customer-owned domains
  • Network proxy rewriting hostname so RemoteUrl is empty
  • CDN/Akamai POP not in allow list serving OneDrive content
  • Mock OneDrive endpoint in lab environments
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("OneDrive.exe","OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe","OneDriveSetup.exe","explorer.exe","services.exe","userinit.exe"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Dump OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe memory and YARA-scan for SPECTRALVIPER strings; check whether the parent process is the legit OneDrive launcher chain (OneDrive.exe → OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe) or something else. Step 2 (contain): Isolate host, kill PID, block destination IP/domain at proxy and EDR-block until verdict. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the destination IP — search every host that contacted it in last 30d. Cross-check for DtlCrashCatch.dll on the same hosts (UC #2).
let Allow = dynamic(["microsoft.com","microsoftonline.com","live.com","office.com","onedrive.com","sharepoint.com","msftncsi.com","msocdn.com","officeapps.live.com","oneclient.sfx.ms"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where isempty(RemoteUrl) or not(RemoteUrl has_any (Allow))
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName =~ "OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe"
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe","OneDriveSetup.exe","OneDrive.exe","explorer.exe","services.exe","svchost.exe")

SPECTRALVIPER C2 beaconing — financemachinelearning.com / gatewayrvcenter.com and IOC IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound communication to the SPECTRALVIPER C2 infrastructure named in the ESET writeup (financemachinelearning[.]com, gatewayrvcenter[.]com plus four other OceanLotus domains and eight IPs). Any contact from a Windows host in the Vietnam SOC scope is high-fidelity given these are dedicated attacker infrastructure. Rationale: Article + IOC bundle list financemachinelearning.com and gatewayrvcenter.com as SPECTRALVIPER C2 plus four sibling OceanLotus domains and eight infrastructure IPs. These are dedicated attacker assets; any internal host contact is a near-certain compromise indicator. Cross-checked OceanLotus infrastructure against MITRE G0050 and ThreatFox. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0050/ • https://threatfox.abuse.ch/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC analyst testing IOC ingestion against a passive DNS replay
  • Threat-intel platform performing meta-resolution of the IOCs
  • Sandbox detonation of the sample inside the corporate range
  • Researcher fetching the C2 for analysis from a controlled VM
  • Network monitoring tap re-injecting historical pcap
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the host is in the Vietnamese stock/investor user persona scope and identify the initiating process — anything other than OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe (UC #3) suggests a different variant. Step 2 (contain): Sinkhole the domains at internal DNS and add IPs to perimeter blocklist, isolate host, capture full PCAP + memory before remediation. Step 3 (hunt): Look back 90 days across the fleet for any of the six domains / eight IPs, pivot on JA3/SNI to find sibling infrastructure, and check for the SPECTRALVIPER SHA1s on identified hosts.

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where RemoteIP in (SVIPs) or RemoteUrl has_any (SVDomains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc

Public-facing MSSQL exploitation — sqlservr.exe spawning cmd/powershell to drop SPECTRALVIPER AIExploitation High
Hunts the second OceanLotus campaign's initial-access path against the Vietnamese infrastructure / transport construction firm: suspected RCE against public-facing Microsoft SQL Server followed by xp_cmdshell-style child-process spawning to stage the SPECTRALVIPER side-load chain. Internet-exposed MSSQL hosts spawning shells are an extremely strong post-exploitation signal. Rationale: Article attributes the second campaign's initial access to suspected RCE against public-facing MSSQL, which is operationally indistinguishable from xp_cmdshell abuse — sqlservr.exe spawning shells is the canonical telemetry. Pivoted from MITRE T1190 + Sigma's existing MSSQL xp_cmdshell rule but kept the article-specific timeframe and follow-on payload context. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/ • https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.003 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DBA running maintenance scripts via xp_cmdshell (legitimate but should be ticketed)
  • SCCM/Intune deploying SQL patches that shell out
  • Monitoring agent enumerating SQL host config via cmd
  • Backup product launching VSS via cmd from SQL service account
  • Vulnerability scanner agent triggering SQL diagnostics
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$") and not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("sqlmaint","Backup Database","DBCC CHECKDB"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm sqlservr.exe is on an internet-facing host (DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing == true) and pull the full child command-line for IOC extraction. Step 2 (contain): Block inbound 1433/TCP from internet at the perimeter, disable xp_cmdshell on the instance, isolate the SQL host. Step 3 (hunt): Search for outbound contact to SPECTRALVIPER C2 (UC #4), look for DtlCrashCatch.dll writes (UC #2), and audit all SQL accounts for new logins, jobs, or linked-server changes since Nov 2024 (the article's earliest known access date for this victim).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "sqlservr.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","mshta.exe","regsvr32.exe","rundll32.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","ipconfig.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP) by DeviceId
) on DeviceId
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\sqlservr.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith_cs "\\cmd.exe" or NewProcessName endswith_cs "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith_cs "\\pwsh.exe" or NewProcessName endswith_cs "\\bitsadmin.exe" or NewProcessName endswith_cs "\\certutil.exe" or NewProcessName endswith_cs "\\curl.exe" or NewProcessName endswith_cs "\\wget.exe" or NewProcessName endswith_cs "\\mshta.exe" or NewProcessName endswith_cs "\\regsvr32.exe" or NewProcessName endswith_cs "\\rundll32.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SPECTRALVIPER known-hash sweep — ESET-published SHA1 IOCs AIInstallation Medium
Hash-based sweep across the fleet for the five SHA1s ESET attributed to the FireAnt SPECTRALVIPER campaign. Used both as a fleet-wide hunt and an alerting rule — any hit is a direct compromise indicator and warrants immediate triage. Rationale: Article + IOC bundle provide five SHA1s tied to the FireAnt SPECTRALVIPER campaign. Hash-based detection is the highest-fidelity primitive available; any hit is a direct campaign indicator. Cross-referenced against MITRE G0050 SPECTRALVIPER mapping and Elastic's prior research. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0050/ • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/elastic-charms-spectralviper
ATT&CKT1027 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal malware-analysis sandbox detonating the sample
  • Threat-intel team importing IOC bundle into a hash-feed indexer
  • Forensic image of a compromised host attached to an analyst workstation
  • Backup product retaining historical infected files
  • EDR scanner already known to host the IOC for testing
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the SHA1 against the article's IOC list and identify host's role (FireAnt stock-investor persona vs. transport/construction infra). Step 2 (contain): Add hash to EDR custom-block list immediately, isolate host, preserve memory + disk image. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the folder path — OceanLotus reuses staging directories across hosts. Cross-check for OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe injection (UC #3) and SPECTRALVIPER C2 contact (UC #4) across the same fleet.
let SVHashes = dynamic(["865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D","B0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D205D6194","48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918BB028E947","511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39FB","8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B00037"]);

| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source="FileEvent";
let P = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(180d)
| where SHA1 in (SVHashes) or InitiatingProcessSHA1 in (SVHashes)
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, FileName=FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine=ProcessCommandLine, Source="ProcessEvent";
let L = DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(180d)
| where SHA1 in (SVHashes)
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source="ImageLoad";
union isfuzzy=true F, P, L
| order by Timestamp desc
let SVHashes = dynamic(["865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D","B0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D205D6194","48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918BB028E947","511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39FB","8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B00037"]);
ImFileEvent

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D", "B0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D205D6194", "48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918BB028E947", "511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39FB", "8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B00037") or SHA1 in~ ("865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D", "B0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D205D6194", "48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918BB028E947", "511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39FB", "8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B00037") or MD5 in~ ("865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D", "B0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D205D6194", "48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918BB028E947", "511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39FB", "8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B00037")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D", "B0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D205D6194", "48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918BB028E947", "511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39FB", "8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B00037") or SHA1 in~ ("865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D", "B0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D205D6194", "48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918BB028E947", "511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39FB", "8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B00037") or MD5 in~ ("865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D", "B0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D205D6194", "48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918BB028E947", "511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39FB", "8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B00037")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D", "B0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D205D6194", "48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918BB028E947", "511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39FB", "8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B00037"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] FireAnt Metakit updater spawning unexpected child processes (supply-chain hunt)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — OceanLotus: From external espionage to domestic targeting
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SPECTRALVIPER DLL side-load: DtlCrashCatch.dll injecting OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe · [LLM] OceanLotus renamed SysInternals ProcDump masquerading as windbg.exe · [LLM] SPECTRALVIPER sample hash hunt across process and file telemetry · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] OceanLotus SPECTRALVIPER C2 infrastructure (domains/IPs from 2024-2026 campaigns) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains · DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
OceanLotus SPECTRALVIPER C2 infrastructure (domains/IPs from 2024-2026 campaigns) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts beacons from any host to the SPECTRALVIPER C&C domains and IPs ESET tied to the FireAnt Metakit supply-chain attack and the Vietnamese infrastructure-construction intrusion. High fidelity because these are dedicated APT32 infrastructure published by ESET and corroborated by Elastic Security Labs / The Hacker News. Rationale: All 6 domains and 8 IPs are listed verbatim in the ESET writeup IOC tables. Corroborated against Elastic Security Labs' original SPECTRALVIPER report and The Hacker News coverage (thehackernews.com/2026/06/oceanlotus-hits-vietnam-investors-with.html). These are dedicated APT32 C2 — any beacon is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/oceanlotus-external-espionage-domestic-targeting/ • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/elastic-charms-spectralviper • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/oceanlotus-hits-vietnam-investors-with.html • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0050/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sinkhole / threat-intel research box deliberately resolving the domains for analysis
  • Internal threat-hunting / honey-call sensors
  • Security vendor sandbox detonations on managed endpoints
  • Stale shared-hosting IP reuse where 139.99.33.239 / OVH ranges legitimately host other tenants long after OceanLotus has rotated
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") and AccountName has_any ("thunt","soc","research"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pivot from RemoteIP/RemoteUrl back to InitiatingProcessFileName + InitiatingProcessCommandLine to identify the host process — is it OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe, a renamed signed binary, or a FireAnt updater child? Pull the parent chain and SHA1/SHA256 for VT lookup. Step 2 (contain): Network-isolate the device via Defender MDE 'Isolate device' action, block the resolved IP at perimeter, and preserve memory before reboot for SPECTRALVIPER's in-memory payload. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all DeviceImageLoadEvents for DtlCrashCatch.dll, all DeviceProcessEvents where ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName matches procdump variants but FileName does not, and any other host that resolved the same C2 domain in the last 90 days.

let SVIPs = dynamic(["139.180.128.42","139.99.33.239","166.88.77.186","103.119.47.104","139.162.11.152","142.91.98.77","38.60.245.37","194.68.26.241"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (SVIPs)
   or RemoteUrl has_any (SVDomains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Protocol, ReportId
| order by Timestamp desc
let SVDomains = dynamic(["gatewayrvcenter.com","coachcybersecurity.com","mxprodesign.com","power-sync-services.com","financemachinelearning.com","leadingfilipinoteams.com"]);
let SVIPs = dynamic(["139.180.128.42","139.99.33.239","166.88.77.186","103.119.47.104","139.162.11.152","142.91.98.77","38.60.245.37","194.68.26.241"]);

  (CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DestinationIP in (SVIPs) or DestinationHostName has_any (SVDomains) | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationPort, RequestURL),
  (DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Name has_any (SVDomains) | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode),
  (ImNetworkSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DstIpAddr in (SVIPs) or DstHostname has_any (SVDomains) | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SPECTRALVIPER DLL side-load: DtlCrashCatch.dll injecting OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe AIInstallation High
Hunts the SPECTRALVIPER loader chain: a legitimate signed binary side-loads a rogue DtlCrashCatch.dll, which then injects into OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe to execute the backdoor in a trusted process. The DLL filename is APT32-specific and the OneDrive sync-service injection target is unusual for any benign software. Rationale: `DtlCrashCatch.dll` and the OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe injection target are named explicitly in the Hacker News writeup and the Elastic Security Labs report on SPECTRALVIPER. Both are non-standard strings — DtlCrashCatch is not a Microsoft DLL and OneDrive's signed sync-service is rarely a CreateRemoteThread/injection target outside this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/oceanlotus-hits-vietnam-investors-with.html • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/elastic-charms-spectralviper • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/oceanlotus-external-espionage-domestic-targeting/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1055.001 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Microsoft Delivery Optimization or telemetry components that happen to share the DtlCrashCatch naming convention (verify Microsoft signature + Authenticode chain)
  • Legitimate OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe launched by OneDrive.exe in C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\Microsoft\OneDrive — the query filters parent==OneDrive.exe out
  • Endpoint research/sandbox detonation that intentionally loaded the sample
  • Memory-analysis tooling (e.g. WinDbg, x64dbg) loading a captured sample for reverse-engineering
Suppression filter
| where DLLSHA1 !in ("<microsoft-signed-hashes-if-any-emerge>") and LoaderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\Microsoft"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Capture the loader binary that side-loaded DtlCrashCatch.dll — its SHA1/SHA256 and Authenticode signer. Cross-check against the ESET sample list (e.g. 41CB8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B0 et al.). Confirm DtlCrashCatch.dll is not Microsoft-signed. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the device, kill OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe and the parent loader process, preserve a memory dump (SPECTRALVIPER is in-memory), and submit DLL + loader to the malware team. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep DeviceFileEvents for DtlCrashCatch.dll writes 30 days back, look at neighbouring files dropped to the same folder (loader EXE), and pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents from OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe to surface SPECTRALVIPER C2.
let LoaderDLL = "DtlCrashCatch.dll";
let InjectTarget = "OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe";
let LoadEvents = DeviceImageLoadEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName =~ LoaderDLL or FolderPath endswith strcat(@"\", LoaderDLL)
  | project LoadTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, DLLPath=FolderPath, DLLSHA1=SHA1, LoaderProc=InitiatingProcessFileName, LoaderPath=InitiatingProcessFolderPath, LoaderCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, LoaderSHA1=InitiatingProcessSHA1, InitiatingProcessAccountName;
let InjectEvents = DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName =~ InjectTarget
  | where InitiatingProcessFileName !~ "OneDrive.exe" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains @"\Microsoft\OneDrive\"
  | project InjectTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, OneDriveCmd=ProcessCommandLine, OneDriveParent=InitiatingProcessFileName, OneDriveParentPath=InitiatingProcessFolderPath;
LoadEvents
| union InjectEvents
| order by LoadTime desc, InjectTime desc
let LoaderDLL = "DtlCrashCatch.dll";
let InjectTarget = "OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe";
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImFileEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where TargetFileName =~ LoaderDLL or TargetFilePath endswith strcat(@"\", LoaderDLL) | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA1, Source="file_event"),
  (ImProcessCreate | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where TargetProcessName =~ InjectTarget | where ParentProcessName !~ "OneDrive.exe" | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, Source="process_create"),
  (SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where EventID == 4688 | where NewProcessName endswith strcat(@"\", InjectTarget) | where ParentProcessName !endswith @"\OneDrive.exe" | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account=SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, Source="sec_4688")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OceanLotus renamed SysInternals ProcDump masquerading as windbg.exe AIInstallation High
Hunts the SPECTRALVIPER stager pattern where OceanLotus copies/renames the legitimately signed Sysinternals ProcDump utility to windbg.exe (or other names) to load an unsigned DONUTLOADER DLL. Pivots on the mismatch between the PE OriginalFileName and the on-disk filename. Rationale: The renamed-ProcDump-as-windbg trick is described in both the ESET writeup and the prior Elastic Security Labs SPECTRALVIPER report. Anchoring on PE OriginalFileName=procdump* with FileName!=procdump* is a high-fidelity OPSEC-tell that catches the masquerade even when the attacker varies the cover name. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/oceanlotus-external-espionage-domestic-targeting/ • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/elastic-charms-spectralviper • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0050/
ATT&CKT1036.003 T1218 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IR / DFIR analyst running a renamed ProcDump for evidence collection (e.g. dump-lsass.exe wrapper) — common in vendor playbooks
  • Sysmon/EDR-driven memory-dump automation that ships ProcDump under a campaign-specific filename
  • Veeam / backup tools repackaging ProcDump inside a vendor-named binary
  • Sysadmins copying ProcDump to a tools directory under a generic name like dump.exe
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("ir-analyst","dfir-svc") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("crowdstrike-falcon.exe","defendpoint.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Capture the renamed binary's SHA256 and Authenticode chain — confirm the certificate matches Microsoft Sysinternals. Inspect the command line for an unsigned DLL load hint (e.g. `-accepteula`, `-ma <pid>`, or DLL paths). Step 2 (contain): Pull the binary, the sibling DLL it side-loaded (likely DONUTLOADER), and isolate the host. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to DeviceImageLoadEvents from this PID for unsigned DLLs loaded out of the same folder, then to DeviceNetworkEvents to surface SPECTRALVIPER beacons (overlap with UC1).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName in~ ("procdump.exe","procdump64.exe","Procdump")
| where FileName !in~ ("procdump.exe","procdump64.exe")
| where ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Sysinternals" or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Procdump"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA1, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessFileOriginalName in~ ("procdump.exe","procdump64.exe","Procdump")
| where ActingProcessName !endswith @"\procdump.exe" and ActingProcessName !endswith @"\procdump64.exe"
| where ActingProcessFileCompany has "Sysinternals"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessFileOriginalName, ActingProcessFileCompany, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SPECTRALVIPER sample hash hunt across process and file telemetry AIInstallation Medium
Sweeps endpoint telemetry for the 20 SHA1 hashes ESET attributes to SPECTRALVIPER and its loaders observed in the 2024-2026 FireAnt / construction-corp campaigns. Catches a hit even when the attacker renames the binary or hides it behind a side-load. Rationale: All 20 SHA1s are listed verbatim in the ESET IOC block. Cross-checked against the Hacker News / Cyberpress writeups which cite the same campaign. Hash-based detection is the lowest-FP control we can deploy against SPECTRALVIPER samples until they rotate. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/oceanlotus-external-espionage-domestic-targeting/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/oceanlotus-hits-vietnam-investors-with.html • https://cyberpress.org/oceanlotus-hits-stock-investors/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1027 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AV / EDR vendor sandbox detonating a captured sample on a managed lab host
  • Threat-intel team intentionally executing the sample in a quarantined network
  • ESET's own telemetry feed re-surfacing the hash via reputation downloads
  • Legitimate sibling Sysinternals or Microsoft binary that ESET miscategorised (low probability — verify Authenticode if hit)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): On any hit, pull the full process tree (parent + grandparent), Authenticode signing chain of every binary in that tree, and the SHA256 (the article gives SHA1 — convert at hit time). Step 2 (contain): Isolate the device, block the SHA1/SHA256 in MDE Indicators, and block the C2 list (UC1). Pull a memory image — SPECTRALVIPER lives in-memory in OneDrive.Sync.Service.exe. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot from the executing user's mailbox to look for the FireAnt Metakit installer download (March 2026 supply-chain window), and run UC2/UC3/UC4 across the same host's 90-day timeline.

union isfuzzy=true
  (DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(90d) | where SHA1 in (SVHashes) or InitiatingProcessSHA1 in (SVHashes) | project Timestamp, Source="Process", DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA1),

| order by Timestamp desc
